name: Amy Woods
body:
There is a belief I run into constantly, in almost every conversation with a B2B marketing leader, which is that their content problem is fundamentally a creation problem, that if they could only produce more of it, or produce it faster, the growth they are looking for would follow, and after ten years of running an agency built entirely around the opposite premise, I have come to think this belief is not just wrong but actively expensive, because it sends companies chasing volume when the actual leak in the system sits somewhere else entirely.

Across three hundred and forty-five episodes of one podcast, and however many more of the second, the pattern I keep returning to in conversation after conversation with B2B marketers is that most teams are sitting on far more usable material than they realize, produced at real expense, and simply letting the majority of its value evaporate after a single use, because nobody on the team owns the job of asking what else this webinar, this podcast, this keynote could become once the live moment has passed.

I think about a conversation I had a while back with a marketing leader at a mid-sized SaaS company, who told me, somewhat sheepishly, that their team had recorded eleven customer webinars that year, each one requiring real coordination to schedule, real preparation to run, and real production cost to record properly, and every single one of them had been watched by its live audience and then filed away, untouched, the moment the recording stopped. Eleven webinars. Eleven pieces of genuinely useful material, produced at genuine expense, treated as disposable the moment their original purpose was served.

That is not a creation problem. It's not even, strictly speaking, a resourcing problem, because the resources to create eleven webinars clearly existed. It is a much narrower and more fixable problem: nobody in that organization had been assigned the job of asking, systematically, what a piece of content could become after its first use, and so the answer defaulted to nothing, eleven times in a row, without anyone deciding that outcome on purpose.

Creating more is not the fix, and I'd go further: for most B2B teams past their first year or two of operating, creating more is close to the last thing they should be spending on. Extracting more from what already exists almost always is the higher-leverage move, and the teams who internalize that distinction tend to spend the next year looking, from the outside, like they've somehow tripled their content output, when in fact they've mostly gotten serious, for the first time, about not wasting what they already had sitting in a recordings folder nobody had opened since the live call ended.

The uncomfortable part of this argument is that it implicates a hiring decision more than a budget line. Most content teams are staffed to create, because creation is the visible, celebrated half of the job, and almost none of them are staffed to systematically mine what's already been made, because that work looks, from the outside, like doing less rather than more, even when it's the half generating the actual return.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
A growing number of executives are coming to us after unsuccessful attempts to elevate their presence on LinkedIn by hiring external writers or agencies to articulate their voice. In most cases, this results not just in underperformance, but in outcomes that actively work "against their objectives".

In short: their standing would have been better preserved had they opted not to publish at all.

This observation may seem counterintuitive, yet it reflects a broader reality of today’s B2B communication environment.

Before allocating more time, budget, or external resources to LinkedIn, it is worth grounding in a few key principles:

1. We are living in an age of extreme overcommunication. Millions of pieces of content are produced each day, and advances in artificial intelligence have reduced the friction required to generate an endless stream of content. In such an environment, restraint carries more value than participation that is poorly conceived (i.e., misaligned with the brand it represents).

2. The underlying problem is not just a lack of effort. More often, it is a failure to begin in the right place. Most agencies and writers approach brand communication on LinkedIn as a publishing exercise. The process begins with the wrong premise: "What should we post today?" But brand communication starts with positioning: "Where and how you stand in the mind of your prospect."

At its simplest, it is the structured placement of aligned signals into a consistent frame until the market or prospect begins to associate you with a singular, high-value outcome. Positioning informs the narrative. The narrative shapes the message. Only then should individual pieces of communication take form. Reversing this sequence is the most common error and carries tangible consequences.

3. None of this suggests that marketing should be rigid. The most effective marketers routinely challenge conventions and reshape expectations. However, there are principles, and there are principles in practice. The best marketers understand how things work in practice. Know the rules so they can be applied intelligently.

4. Technical writing ability, while essential, is only one component of effective executive communication. At its highest level, executive communication sits at the intersection of strategy, positioning, and narrative discipline.

5. And here’s the thing… there isn’t really a fifth point. Remember the good old days of marketing when an "odd number of tips" was a rule? Well, the good old days of marketing are gone, and it no longer requires arbitrary symmetry.

name: Amy Woods
body:
Somewhere around episode two hundred of doing this, interviewing B2B marketers about how they actually run content operations rather than how they'd describe it in a case study, I stopped being surprised by a particular kind of answer, which is that the marketers with the most polished output are rarely the ones with the biggest budgets, and are almost always the ones with the clearest internal definition of what a piece of content is actually supposed to do before a single word of it gets written.

The teams without that clarity produce content that is, individually, often quite good, well-designed, well-written, occasionally even clever, and collectively incoherent, because each piece was optimized for its own moment rather than for a role in something larger, and a buyer scrolling past six months of that output could not tell you, from the feed alone, what the company actually believes about its category.

I remember one guest in particular, running content for a well-funded SaaS company, who described her team's process with genuine pride: a content calendar filled a quarter in advance, every slot assigned a format and a topic, every piece shipped on schedule without exception. It sounded, by any conventional measure, like a well-run operation, and in a narrow sense it was. But when I asked her what her company's single most important belief about its category was, the thing every piece of content should ultimately be reinforcing, she paused for long enough that the answer was obvious before she said a word. The calendar was full. The point of view underneath it was not.

That gap is more common than most marketing leaders would admit publicly, and it explains something I've noticed across nearly every high-output, low-impact content operation I've encountered on this podcast: the problem was never a shortage of discipline. These teams were disciplined enough to hit every deadline for years. The problem was that discipline had been applied to a schedule instead of to a belief, and a schedule, however faithfully followed, cannot manufacture a point of view it was never built to carry in the first place.

The fix is rarely more creative talent, and it's almost never more budget either, both of which are the two solutions most executives reach for first when content isn't landing. It is almost always a documented point of view that every subsequent piece of content is required to serve, however small that piece might be, tested against a simple question before anything ships: does this asset make our specific belief about the category clearer to someone reading it, or does it simply exist, competently, alongside everything else already in their feed. The agencies and in-house teams who build that discipline in early tend to spend far less time actually producing content, and far more time upfront deciding, deliberately, what each piece is for before a single designer or writer touches it.

name: Amy Woods
body:
Standing on a stage a few weeks ago talking to a room of B2B marketers about repurposing, I said something I hadn't quite planned to say, which was that most content calendars are really just a scheduling problem dressed up as a strategy document, and I watched enough heads nod in that room to know it landed harder than I expected, which usually means I'd stumbled onto something people already suspected privately but hadn't heard said out loud.

A calendar tells you when something is going out. It rarely tells you why that particular piece, in that particular format, at that particular moment, is the right use of the underlying material, and the gap between those two things is exactly where most B2B content operations quietly lose the return they were promised when the budget got approved in the first place.

Afterward, during the Q&A, someone in the audience asked the question I probably should have anticipated, which was: fine, but what does the alternative actually look like in practice, day to day, rather than as a slogan on a slide. It's a fair challenge, because "have a point of view" is easy to say and considerably harder to operationalize inside a real marketing team with real deadlines and a real content calendar that still, at the end of the day, needs to get filled.

The honest answer I gave, and the one I'd still stand behind, is that it looks less dramatic than people expect. It looks like a short, specific document, maintained and revisited monthly rather than written once and filed away, that states plainly what the company believes about its category that most competitors either don't believe or won't say out loud, and every subsequent piece of content, before it's greenlit, gets checked against that document rather than against whether it's due on the calendar that week. It is not a bigger workload. It is the same workload, redirected, with a five-minute check added at the start of the process rather than skipped entirely in the rush to fill the next open slot.

What I told that room, and what I'd say again here, is that the question worth asking before any calendar gets built is not "what do we publish this week," but "what have we already created that we haven't finished getting value from yet, and does our point of view actually show up clearly in it," because in nine cases out of ten, for a B2B company that has been operating for more than a year or two, the honest answer to the first half of that question is: quite a lot, and the honest answer to the second half is the more uncomfortable one worth sitting with.

I've since started asking every guest on this podcast some version of that same question, and the pattern holds up more consistently than almost anything else I track across these conversations: the marketers who answer quickly, without needing to think, tend to run operations that outperform their budget. The ones who pause, the way that guest in the audience's own team might have, are usually the ones whose content calendar is fuller than their category conviction, and no amount of additional scheduling discipline closes that particular gap.

name: Ann Jhelica Cruz
body:
We took a single client webinar recording last week, fifty-one minutes long, moderately well attended live, and by Friday it had become a LinkedIn carousel, three short-form video clips, a blog post, a set of quote cards, an infographic, and two audiograms, and I want to walk through the actual decisions behind that, because "we repurpose content" is a sentence that means almost nothing until you see the choices underneath it.

The carousel wasn't built from the most quotable moment in the recording, which is the instinct most people would follow. It was built from the moment where the guest contradicted a piece of conventional wisdom in the room, because contradiction travels further on this platform than agreement ever does, and a carousel's job is to stop a scroll, not to summarize a talk. We tested this against the more obviously quotable line first, in an earlier draft, and it read fine, competent, forgettable. The contradiction version, by contrast, made two people on our own team stop and argue about whether they agreed with it, which is usually the signal that it'll do the same thing in someone else's feed.

The blog post, by contrast, kept almost none of that contradiction as its opening, because a reader arriving from search is looking for an answer, not a debate, and burying the useful information under a rhetorical hook that worked beautifully on LinkedIn would have cost us the reader within four seconds of a Google search landing. Instead it opened with the actual question the webinar answered, stated plainly, and saved the more provocative framing for a pull-quote three paragraphs in, once the reader had already decided to stay.

The audiograms took the longest to get right, which surprised even us. Video and text both let you cut around an awkward pause or a half-finished sentence with a visual transition; audio alone has nowhere to hide, so the fifteen seconds we eventually used took four attempts to find, each one technically accurate to what was said but rhythmically wrong for a standalone clip until the fourth pass landed.

Same source material, same underlying insight, five entirely different jobs across five different formats, and treating any two of them as interchangeable is exactly how repurposing becomes the shallow, mechanical thing most people assume it is when they hear the word for the first time.

What's easy to miss from the outside is that none of these five decisions took longer than the original creative brief anticipated, because the mapping happens before production starts, not during it. By the time anyone on the creative team touches the recording, we already know which format is being aimed at which platform and why, which means the actual making of each asset is fast precisely because none of the harder thinking is happening in the moment, under deadline, the way it would if we were figuring out the plan and executing it simultaneously.

name: Ann Jhelica Cruz
body:
We killed a piece of creative this week that, by every visual standard, looked genuinely good, clean, on-brand, well-typeset, and I want to talk about why, because the reasoning matters more than the outcome, and it's the kind of decision that never shows up in a portfolio even though it's some of the more important work we do.

The infographic in question summarized a client's five-step framework accurately and attractively, and it would have sailed through review at most agencies without a second look. It didn't survive ours, because the framework it summarized wasn't actually the client's most defensible point of view; it was a reasonably generic five-step model that a dozen competitors could have produced with minor edits, and no amount of design craft changes that underlying fact. You can typeset a forgettable idea beautifully. It stays forgettable. It just takes an extra beat for someone to notice.

The harder part of this decision wasn't recognizing the problem, which took about ninety seconds once we sat with it honestly. It was going back to the client with that feedback, because from their side, they'd approved that five-step framework months earlier, in a different meeting, for different reasons, and telling them the asset built from it wasn't worth shipping meant implicitly questioning a decision they'd already signed off on. That conversation is uncomfortable in a way that just quietly shipping the pretty infographic would never have been, and I understand completely why most agencies choose the quiet option instead.

We had it anyway, and the actual client reaction surprised us: relief, more than defensiveness, because somewhere in the back of their mind they'd already half-suspected the framework was a bit generic, and having someone say so plainly, backed by a concrete alternative rather than just a criticism, gave them permission to fix something they'd been quietly unhappy with for a while.

Good design dressed around a forgettable idea is still forgettable; it just takes longer to notice, and by the time it's noticed, the client has usually spent real money finding that out the slow way. The job of the creative team here isn't only to make things look considered. It's to notice, before the client ever sees a draft, when the underlying idea doesn't deserve the polish we're about to spend on it, and to say so clearly enough that it can actually be acted on, which is a harder and less comfortable service than most people are paying an agency for, and also, in our experience, the one that actually earns a second year of the relationship.

We've since built a quiet version of this check into how every brief gets reviewed before production starts, not as a formal gate that slows things down, but as a single question someone on the creative team has to answer honestly before touching a design file: if a competitor could produce this exact idea with minor edits, is the design alone going to be what makes it worth the client's time. More often than we'd like to admit, the honest answer is no, and it's cheaper for everyone to hear that at the brief stage than at the invoice stage.

name: Ann Jhelica Cruz
body:
A quote card looks like the easiest asset we make. Pull a sentence, put it on a background, ship it. I want to explain why that's almost never how it actually goes, using one we made this week as the example, because the gap between how simple this looks from outside and how much thinking actually goes into thirty seconds of work is one of the things people underestimate most about this job.

The sentence we ultimately used wasn't the most obviously quotable line in the recording, the one with the cleanest rhythm and the biggest reaction from the live audience. It was a quieter, more specific sentence three minutes later that most people listening back would probably scroll past, because the flashier line, taken out of its original context, read as a platitude the moment you removed the speaker's tone and timing from around it. On the page, stripped of the room's energy, it said something that could have come from almost any speaker at almost any conference, which is exactly the failure mode a good quote card exists to avoid.

We ran both through what's become an informal test on this team, which is simply reading the card out loud, cold, to someone who wasn't in the room for the original recording, and watching whether they nodded because it sounded good or because it actually meant something specific to them. The flashier line got a nod of the first kind, polite, a little empty. The quieter line got someone asking a follow-up question, which is the reaction that actually tells you an idea survived the trip from a live room onto a static image.

The quieter line held up alone. That's the actual test for whether something belongs on a card: not whether it sounded good in the room, but whether it survives being stripped of every piece of context that made it land the first time, and a surprising amount of genuinely good spoken content fails that test the instant you try to lift it onto a static image, precisely because so much of what made it land depended on delivery rather than on the words themselves.

This is, I think, the part of repurposing that's hardest to explain to someone who hasn't sat through the process, and the reason a thirty-second quote card can take longer to get right than a five-minute video, because a video can still lean on tone and pacing to carry a line the words alone wouldn't quite hold up, whereas a static card has nothing else to lean on and has to succeed on the sentence alone.

It's also, I'd argue, the clearest single test of whether a piece of content actually had something to say in the first place, rather than simply sounding good in the moment it was delivered. Plenty of genuinely energetic, well-received talks turn out, once you try to extract a standalone card from them, to contain very little that survives outside the room, and that's useful information in itself: it tells you the value of that particular recording lived almost entirely in the delivery, and any repurposing plan for it needs to lean on video and audio formats rather than static ones, because text is where thin content gets found out fastest.

name: Alison Rodd
body:
A new client project doesn't start with a creative brainstorm here, whatever people might assume from the outside. It starts with an intake document that maps every existing content asset the client has, podcast archive, webinar recordings, past decks, sales call transcripts if they're willing to share them, against the verticals and formats we already know convert for companies like theirs, and it's the least visible piece of every engagement despite being, in my view, the piece that determines almost everything downstream.

That mapping takes two to three days before a single piece of creative gets touched, and it is, without question, the least glamorous part of the entire engagement. Nobody has ever asked to sit in on this stage; clients are, understandably, much more interested in seeing the first carousel or the first video clip than in watching someone build a spreadsheet of every recording they've made since 2019. But it's the part of the process that determines whether everything downstream runs smoothly or turns into a slow-motion scramble around week six, once the easy, obvious repurposing opportunities have been used up and nobody documented what was left.

I can point to a specific project where skipping a proper version of this mapping, early in the agency's history before we'd formalized the process, cost us about three weeks of rework. The team started producing against whatever material felt immediately obvious, without a full inventory, and by week five had exhausted the recordings that felt easy to work with while a folder of older, less obviously usable material sat untouched, unmapped, and effectively invisible to the creative team who didn't know it existed. We rebuilt the intake process specifically because of that project, and it's the reason no engagement since has started without it.

Clients rarely see this stage directly, which is by design; what they see is a delivery schedule that holds, week after week, without the usual mid-project renegotiation of scope that tends to happen at agencies who skipped this step to get to the fun part faster. The two to three days spent mapping at the start of an engagement is, in effect, the reason the following twelve months don't require a difficult conversation about why the content ran out sooner than anyone expected.

I've come to think of this as the actual product we're selling, more than any individual piece of creative that gets shipped. A client can, in principle, ask a freelancer to turn one recording into a carousel for considerably less than what we charge, and that comparison is fair as far as it goes. What a freelancer isn't positioned to do is map an entire archive against a twelve-month plan before day one, which is the part of the work that prevents the whole engagement from quietly running out of runway just as it's starting to build momentum with an audience.

name: Alison Rodd
body:
Every asset that leaves this building passes through the same three-person check before a client ever sees it, and I want to describe what each of those three checks is actually looking for, because "we have a QA process" is a claim almost every agency makes and almost none of them can describe specifically, which usually means it lives entirely in one person's head and disappears the day that person takes a holiday.

The first check is factual: does this asset accurately represent what was actually said or shown in the source material, with nothing exaggerated or quietly smoothed over in the edit. This sounds obvious until you watch how easily a well-intentioned edit for clarity can drift into a mild overstatement of what a speaker actually claimed, especially once a quote has passed through a design file and a caption writer and lost some of its original hedging along the way.

The second check is brand: does the tone, terminology, and visual treatment match what this specific client has approved before, rather than what our house style would default to if left unchecked. We work across four fairly different verticals, and the tone that lands for a Wealth Management client would read as jarringly casual for an HR Tech client and oddly clinical for a fast-moving SaaS brand, so this check exists specifically to catch a creative team, however talented, defaulting to what feels natural to them rather than what's actually right for the account in front of them.

The third check, and the one most agencies skip, is format-fit: is this asset actually suited to the platform and audience it's headed for, or is it a repackaged version of something that worked somewhere else being shipped here out of convenience. We caught eleven issues across those three checks last month before anything reached a client, none of them dramatic individually, a slightly overstated claim here, an off-brand phrase there, one video edited for a platform's aspect ratio but not its typical viewing behavior, all of them the kind of small miss that, left uncaught, erodes trust in an agency over a year of accumulation rather than in any single embarrassing moment a client would ever actually notice or complain about directly.

What makes this check hard to justify to a client who's never seen the alternative is that its value is almost entirely invisible when it's working correctly. A client whose content has passed through this process cleanly for a year has no comparison point for what would have shipped without it, and so the check tends to get treated as overhead rather than as the thing actually protecting the relationship, right up until the one time it's skipped and something goes out that shouldn't have, at which point its absence becomes very visible very quickly, usually in the form of an awkward client email that a properly staffed check would have prevented entirely.

name: Alison Rodd
body:
I want to walk through what a single Tuesday looks like for one of our accounts, because "turnaround time" is a number on a proposal until you see what actually produces it, and I think most clients would find the actual mechanics more reassuring than the number alone ever manages to be.

Morning starts with reviewing what came in from the client over the weekend, usually a recorded call or a piece of feedback on last week's batch, and slotting it against the production calendar for that account. This sounds routine, and mostly it is, but it's also the point in the week where a small miscommunication, if there's going to be one, tends to surface: a piece of feedback that reads two different ways depending on how you interpret one ambiguous sentence, and catching that ambiguity on a Tuesday morning is considerably cheaper than catching it on a Thursday afternoon once a designer has already built three assets around the wrong interpretation.

Midday is spent in the actual review queue, checking assets against the three-part QA process before they move to client approval. On a typical Tuesday that's somewhere between six and ten individual pieces moving through, each one a few minutes of focused attention rather than a rushed glance, because the whole point of having dedicated time blocked for this is that it doesn't get done in the gaps between other tasks, where things get missed.

Afternoon is reserved for the handoff conversation with whoever wrote that week's briefs, making sure nothing is queued for production without a clear instruction behind it, because a beautifully executed asset built from an unclear brief is still a miss, just a more expensive one to fix once a designer has already spent real hours on it. This conversation usually takes fifteen minutes and prevents, by my own rough estimate, at least one wasted production cycle most weeks.

None of this is especially dramatic to describe, which is rather the point. The accounts that run smoothly are the ones where a day like this happens quietly, every day, without anyone outside operations ever needing to notice it was happening at all, and the accounts that don't run smoothly are usually missing exactly one of these three checkpoints, quietly, for long enough that nobody notices until the delivery schedule starts slipping for reasons nobody can quite point to.

I've started keeping rough notes on which of the three checkpoints tends to slip first when an account is under pressure, because it's rarely random. It's almost always the midday review queue, since it's the one block of time that looks, on a busy day, most dispensable to skip in favor of something that feels more urgent. It never is dispensable, and the accounts where I've had to fight hardest to protect that block are, without exception, the ones that have gone the longest without a client ever needing to ask us what happened to a piece of content that was supposed to ship that week.

name: Harry Goossens
body:
A brief that says "repurpose this webinar into social content" is not a brief, whatever a client's original request might have looked like when it landed in our inbox, and most of my job, if I'm honest about it, is the unglamorous work of turning a request like that into something a creative can actually act on without guessing, which is a less visible skill than writing or design but breaks the whole system just as badly when it's missing.

A usable brief for us specifies which three or four moments in the source material are the strongest candidates for repurposing and why, which platform each resulting asset is aimed at and what that platform's audience actually does differently with content, and what the client has previously rejected in this format so nobody repeats a mistake that's already been made once. Strip any one of those three things out and the brief technically exists but doesn't actually do its job, which is to prevent the same clarifying question from being asked three times across three different people before a single asset gets made.

I can point to a specific week, early on, before I'd tightened this process, where a single missing detail in a brief, we hadn't noted that a client's legal team required a specific disclaimer on any content mentioning pricing, cost us a redo on four separate assets, because the same gap in the brief had been copied across all four without anyone catching it until a client flagged it on delivery. That one miss changed how every brief gets built now: a dedicated section for anything the client has flagged as sensitive or restricted, checked explicitly before a brief is considered finished, not assumed to be common knowledge that everyone on the team already has memorized.

Writing a brief like this takes longer than writing "repurpose this into social content," obviously, usually somewhere between twenty and forty minutes depending on how much of the source material needs a first pass before the strongest moments are even identifiable. But that time gets paid back many times over across the life of the brief, because a creative working from a genuinely usable brief rarely needs to come back with a clarifying question, and every clarifying question that does get asked costs more collective time, across more people, than the extra twenty minutes it would have taken to answer it upfront.

I've started measuring this loosely, because I was curious whether the extra time upfront actually paid for itself the way I assumed it did. Across a sample of briefs I wrote carefully versus a handful I rushed during a particularly busy stretch last quarter, the rushed briefs generated, on average, just over two clarifying questions each before an asset shipped. The careful ones generated close to zero. Twenty extra minutes at the start, against roughly two rounds of back-and-forth avoided later, is not a close call once you actually total the time on both sides of the ledger.

name: Harry Goossens
body:
Every client engagement starts with a strategy conversation that generates far more ideas than we will ever actually produce, and the part of my job nobody sees is the deliberate work of cutting most of that list down before it ever becomes a production calendar, which is a less comfortable task than it sounds, because it means telling people, including sometimes our own strategists, that an idea they're genuinely excited about isn't going to make the first quarter.

We cut ideas for two different reasons, and it matters which one applies. Some ideas get cut because they're good but not sequenced correctly yet, they'll come back in month two once a foundation of core content exists for them to build on. A carousel series built around a client's most contrarian point of view, for instance, tends to land far better once an audience already has some baseline familiarity with the company's tone, rather than as the very first thing a cold audience ever sees from them.

Others get cut because they sound clever in a strategy call and fall apart the moment you try to actually produce them against a real client's approval process, their brand guidelines, or the amount of raw material actually available to support them. I remember one idea from an early strategy session that everyone in the room genuinely liked: a weekly "myth versus reality" series contrasting industry assumptions with the client's own data. It fell apart within a week of trying to produce it, because the client's data team, once we actually asked, could only support that claim with genuinely fresh figures roughly once a quarter, not weekly, and a series that runs out of real material by week four is worse for the brand than never starting it.

Conflating those two categories is how agencies end up either over-promising in the kickoff deck or quietly under-delivering by month three, and telling a client honestly which category an idea falls into, even when it's a good idea, is most of what keeps a relationship intact past the first quarter. It's a less exciting conversation than pitching the idea in the first place, and it's the one that actually protects the client from a promise we'd have struggled to keep.

What I've learned to do differently since that particular miss is ask the sourcing question earlier, in the strategy call itself rather than a week into production: not "does this idea sound good," which almost everything does in a room full of people excited about a new engagement, but "what specifically would we need from the client's own systems to sustain this past the first month, and has anyone actually confirmed that's available." It's a duller question to ask in a room full of enthusiasm, and it's saved us from at least three ideas since that would otherwise have looked exactly like that myth-versus-reality series once we got a few weeks in, quietly running out of real material before the audience it was aimed at had even fully found it.

name: Harry Goossens
body:
Our standard turnaround from raw recording to first delivered asset sits at five business days, and I want to explain what actually has to happen correctly, in sequence, for that number to hold, because a number like that means nothing without the process underneath it, and I've watched enough clients quote a turnaround time from a proposal without understanding what it actually requires to know it's worth spelling out plainly.

Day one is intake and brief-writing, the stage Alison and I both spend the most time on even though it produces nothing a client can see yet. Days two and three are production, where the actual assets get built against briefs that, if day one went correctly, shouldn't require a single clarifying question along the way. Day four is the three-part QA process, factual accuracy, brand fit, and format fit, run by someone who wasn't involved in producing the asset, because a second set of eyes catches things the person who made it is too close to see. Day five is client delivery and the first round of feedback.

Any single day running long, a brief that needed a second pass because the source recording surfaced a complication nobody anticipated, a source recording with unusable audio that needs a workaround, a client slow to answer a clarifying question that genuinely couldn't be resolved without their input, pushes the entire five-day window, which is why the handoff between each stage matters more than the speed of any individual stage on its own. I've tracked our internal slippage over the past two quarters, and the single most common cause, by a wide margin, isn't production running slow. It's day one running long, because a rushed brief on Monday morning shows up as a delay on Wednesday afternoon that looks, from the outside, like a production problem when it was actually a briefing problem three days earlier.

Turnaround time isn't a promise about how fast any one person works. It's a promise about how cleanly five different handoffs happen in a row, and that's the thing we actually manage, day by day, far more than we manage any individual person's raw output speed.

Once I started tracking slippage by stage rather than treating a missed deadline as one undifferentiated event, the fix became a lot more specific than "everyone move faster." It became: protect day one, specifically, more aggressively than any other stage in the sequence, even if that means a brief occasionally takes closer to forty minutes than twenty. A day one that runs long by twenty minutes is invisible to the client. A day four that runs long because of it shows up as a missed delivery date, and by then the actual cause is three days upstream and much harder to see, let alone explain, if a client asks why a batch came in late that particular week, and "the brief took a bit longer on Monday" is a much less satisfying answer to give three days after the fact than it would have been to hear on Monday itself.

name: Jessica Everitt, MBA, PMP
body:
I've had a strange career path if you look at it from the outside: writing and editing, then process improvement, then project management, then a stint that touched finance, and now I run operations for a fifty-person agency, and none of it looks like a straight line if you were to lay the résumé flat on a table and ask a stranger to guess what came next after any single entry on it. For a long time I assumed that non-linearity was a liability I'd eventually need to explain away in an interview, some awkward story about indecision I'd have to spin into a narrative of intentional growth.

It wasn't a liability. It turned out to be the actual training, and I only recognized that in hindsight, long after I'd already made most of the moves that built it.

Editing teaches you to find the sentence that doesn't earn its place in a paragraph, the one doing decoration rather than work, and you develop that instinct almost without noticing you're developing it. Process improvement teaches you to find the step in a workflow that doesn't earn its place either, and there is more overlap between those two skills than I expected when I first made the jump between them; both are, underneath the surface, the same discipline of asking what's actually necessary versus what merely feels necessary because it's always been there. Project management taught me that a plan nobody can execute under real conditions isn't a plan at all, it's a wish dressed up in a Gantt chart, and I learned that lesson the hard way more than once, watching a beautifully sequenced timeline collapse the moment a single dependency ran even slightly late. And the finance work, which I came to almost accidentally, taught me that every operational decision eventually shows up as a number someone has to stand behind in a meeting, whether or not the person who made the decision was thinking about that number at the time.

I went back and got an MBA and a PMP later, once I already had most of the instincts, which is probably backwards from how most operators build their credentials, and I've since come to think the order actually mattered more than the credentials themselves. I wasn't learning frameworks to apply to a blank page the way a lot of my classmates were. I was learning the proper vocabulary for things I'd already figured out the hard way, running actual client work, which meant the coursework mostly confirmed and sharpened instincts rather than installing new ones from scratch.

If there's a lesson worth pulling out of all this, it's that operations talent doesn't only come from operations roles, however tidy that origin story sounds in a hiring narrative. Some of the best instincts for running a company come from having actually done the unglamorous, easily overlooked work the company depends on first, long before anyone hands you a title that says you're allowed to have opinions about how the whole machine should run.

name: Jessica Everitt, MBA, PMP
body:
"Scaling without killing momentum" is a phrase I use often enough that people on my team probably roll their eyes a little every time it comes out of my mouth in a planning meeting. But I want to be specific about what actually breaks first when a growing agency scales too quickly, because it's rarely the thing leadership tends to worry about most, and the mismatch between the worry and the actual failure point is worth naming plainly.

It's not usually quality, at least not at first. Most growing agencies protect quality fiercely and visibly, because it's the thing clients notice immediately and complain about loudly if it slips, which means it gets defended by instinct even under real growth pressure. What breaks first, quietly, almost invisibly for a quarter or two before anyone names it, is context, the shared understanding of why a particular client operates the way they do, which used to live comfortably in two or three people's heads back when the team was small enough that everyone had touched every account at some point. Nobody explicitly documented that understanding, because there was never a moment where documenting it felt urgent; it was simply there, ambient, available to anyone who needed it because the team was small enough to ask.

I've watched this exact pattern repeat itself often enough now to recognize the early symptom before it fully surfaces: a new account lead asks a question that a founding team member would have answered instinctively, without needing to check anything, and there's a pause in the room before anyone can actually answer it, because the honest answer is "nobody ever wrote that down, we just always knew it." I remember one particular instance where a fairly basic question about a long-standing client's internal approval process sat unanswered for most of a call, not because the information was complicated, but because the one person who'd have known it instantly was out that week, and nothing existed anywhere else that could stand in for her.

The fix isn't more process for its own sake, which is the instinct most operators reach for the moment they sense a gap like this, and it's the instinct I'd actively push back on if I saw someone reaching for it too broadly. The actual fix is being deliberate about which two or three pieces of institutional knowledge, for each individual client, absolutely have to move from someone's head into something durable and searchable before the team grows past the size where tribal knowledge still quietly works. Everything else can stay informal, undocumented, exactly as loose as it's always been, without any real cost. That short, deliberately narrow list is the actual scaling work worth doing, and it's smaller and considerably more specific than most growth plans ever account for when they're drawn up on a whiteboard months before the growth actually happens.

name: Jessica Everitt, MBA, PMP
body:
Six years ago, before Foundation was anywhere near the size it is now, our founder made a decision that had nothing to do with marketing, growth, or clients: the company would close every year to observe Juneteenth. I want to talk about why that particular decision has stuck for six consecutive years, because a lot of commitments made when a company is small and idealistic quietly disappear once the company isn't small anymore and a hundred more urgent priorities have arrived to compete for the same attention.

We're a genuinely global team now, spread across enough countries that plenty of people joining us had never heard of Juneteenth before their first year here, which could easily have become the reason to quietly let the holiday fade into something optional, explained away as "not universally relevant to our team" the way a lot of well-intentioned early commitments eventually get rationalized out of existence as a company scales and diversifies. That hasn't happened, and I think the reason it hasn't is instructive for how culture actually survives growth rather than just getting talked about as something a company values.

Nobody had to re-decide it every single year. It was never framed, even at the start, as a marketing-adjacent gesture that needed to keep justifying its own existence against a return-on-investment conversation. It was simply something we do, presented with the same unremarkable certainty as any other holiday on the calendar, which meant it never had to compete for attention against the dozens of newer, louder priorities that show up every quarter as a company scales into new markets and hires people who've never encountered the original reasoning behind the decision. I've had newer team members ask, genuinely curious rather than skeptical, why we observe it, and the answer that seems to land best isn't a justification at all, it's simply that we always have, and that consistency itself has become part of what makes it feel meaningful rather than performative.

I think about this constantly in my own role now, because operations is full of decisions that either get re-litigated endlessly, revisited every time someone new joins with a different opinion, or become durable enough that nobody has to actively defend them anymore. The commitments that actually survive real growth are rarely the ones defended the loudest in the moment they're made. They're the ones made simple enough, and early enough, and without excessive self-justification, that revisiting them was never seriously on the table to begin with, which is a much quieter kind of durability than most culture initiatives are designed to achieve.

It's a small example against the scale of everything else operations touches, but I keep coming back to it precisely because it's small. It's proof that the mechanism for durable culture isn't grand statements or annual recommitment ceremonies. It's simply making the right call once, early, and then declining to reopen it every time reopening it would have been more convenient than standing by it.

name: James Scherer
body:
I have an English literature degree. Not a marketing degree, not a business degree, English lit, with a minor in history, and for the first several years of my career I genuinely thought that might be a problem I'd eventually need to work around, some credential gap I'd have to compensate for every time I sat across from someone with an actual marketing background on their résumé.

My first real marketing job was in-house at a startup in Vancouver, and nobody there taught me content strategy in any formal sense, because nobody there had a formal sense of it to teach; we were all figuring it out roughly in parallel. I learned it by writing a genuinely large volume of mediocre content, watching carefully what worked and what didn't across dozens of attempts, and slowly building a rough internal model of why, one uncomfortable public failure at a time. The literature degree turned out to matter more than I expected, just not in the way I assumed it would going in. It wasn't that I could write cleaner sentences than someone without it, though that helped at the margins. It was that close-reading a text for what an author was actually doing structurally, underneath the surface, tracking why a particular scene worked and a similar one two chapters later didn't, is disturbingly close to the actual skill of figuring out why one piece of content lands with a reader and an almost identical one doesn't.

I've since led content strategy for companies like monday.com and ActiveCampaign, working with teams considerably larger and more resourced than that first Vancouver startup ever was, and I still think about that early job as the real education, more than any framework, certification, or later mentor ever gave me. Nobody handed me a playbook at the start. I had to build one slowly, by getting things wrong publicly, in front of an actual audience whose indifference or engagement I couldn't argue my way out of, and paying close attention to why the failures failed and the occasional successes worked.

If you're early in this field and quietly worried that your degree or your first job doesn't look like the "right" background for where you want to end up, I'd gently push back on that worry, because I don't think it holds up as well as it feels like it should from the inside. Most of the people I respect most in this industry, the ones whose judgment I actually trust when a strategy decision gets genuinely difficult, got here sideways rather than by some clean, direct path from a marketing degree straight into a marketing career. The sideways route just takes a little longer to explain cleanly at a dinner party, and it's worth remembering that a messy origin story and a weak one are not the same thing at all.

I still catch myself, more than a decade in, reaching for an instinct that traces straight back to a seminar room rather than a marketing course: asking what a piece of writing is actually trying to do before judging whether it's doing it well. That question has proven useful in nearly every content decision I've made since.

name: James Scherer
body:
"SEO is your space, your website, your blog, your technical optimization. GEO is all of that, plus every external source an AI system pulls from to learn about your category." I say some version of this constantly, in client calls and on panels, and I want to unpack the part people usually skip past when they nod along to it: we don't actually optimize for generative engines. We influence them. That's not a rhetorical flourish I reach for because it sounds sharper in a keynote slide. It's a genuinely different mental model for how the actual work gets done, day to day, on a real account.

SEO, at its core, was always a negotiation with a single, known algorithm you could reverse-engineer with enough patience, enough testing, and enough time spent reading Google's own documentation between the lines. GEO isn't that, and treating it as though it were is the single most common mistake I see teams make when they first try to adapt their existing playbook. It's trying to shape what a language model believes to be true and comprehensive about your category, and that model formed its view by reading essentially everything within reach, your site, certainly, but also Reddit threads discussing your competitors, review sites nobody on your team monitors, competitor comparison pages you didn't write and can't edit, community discussions you were never invited into and don't know are happening. You cannot submit a sitemap to any of that. You can only show up, repeatedly and credibly, across enough of the actual places the model is learning from, over enough time that your presence starts to look like consensus rather than a single loud voice.

That's why "Share of Model" is the metric I keep coming back to in nearly every strategy conversation now, instead of the old rankings conversation everyone in this industry was trained to have for two decades. It's not "where do we rank for this term." It's "in how many of the answers this model generates for our category do we actually get mentioned at all, across how many different platforms, phrased how many different ways." If the honest answer to that question is close to zero, you don't have a rankings problem you can fix with better on-page optimization. You don't exist in the model's consideration set yet, full stop, and that is a completely different diagnosis, requiring a completely different fix, than a rankings drop has ever been in the SEO world most of us came up in.

I've watched teams spend real budget trying to "optimize" their way into GEO visibility using tactics lifted directly from an SEO playbook, and it rarely works, because the target isn't a crawler following predictable rules. It's a model forming an impression the same slow way a person does, through repetition, through corroboration across sources, through simply being present often enough in the right places that absence would actually be noticeable.

name: James Scherer
body:
There's a lot I could say about my inability to delegate effectively, and I've decided the honest version of that story is more useful to share here than the polished, already-fixed version most leadership content defaults to.

For years, my instinct under any real pressure was to just quietly take the task back rather than sit through the discomfort of watching someone else do it slower, or noticeably differently, than I would have done it myself. I told myself this was efficiency, a reasonable trade of a few minutes of friction for a faster, cleaner outcome. It wasn't efficiency. It was avoidance, dressed up convincingly enough as a productivity habit that I didn't examine it closely for longer than I'd like to admit, and it quietly capped how much my team could actually grow, because nobody develops real judgment by watching someone else make the final call every single time a decision gets even slightly uncomfortable.

My new goal, stated plainly and a little ridiculously, mostly because naming it seriously felt too self-important: undonkey myself. Which mostly means noticing the exact moment I feel the urge to reach over and take something back, and forcing a deliberate pause instead, long enough to ask whether the person doing the work needs my hand on it, or whether I just need to tolerate ten uncomfortable minutes of not controlling the outcome. I caught myself doing the old version last month, on a deliverable that wasn't shaping up how I'd have written it, the internal negotiation took longer than just letting the draft go out slightly different from how I'd have done it.

I don't think this is a rare flaw among people who came up doing the actual work themselves, writing the content, running the campaigns, before they were ever managing anyone else's output. I think it's an extremely common one that most of us simply don't say out loud, because "I'm still learning to let go" doesn't sound like leadership advice worth putting on a slide. I've come to think it's some of the more useful leadership advice I actually have, precisely because so few people running teams are willing to admit they still need it, years into the job, well past the point where they're supposed to have already solved it.

What's helped more than any single mindset shift is a small, almost mechanical habit: before I intervene, I make myself articulate, out loud or in writing, exactly what would go wrong if I didn't. Half the time, the honest answer is nothing would meaningfully go wrong, it would just look different from how I'd have done it, which is a weaker justification for stepping in than it feels like in the moment. The rest of the time, there's a real risk worth flagging, and articulating it clearly is a better use of my time than quietly redoing the work myself, because it teaches the reasoning rather than just handing back a corrected output with nothing attached to it.

It's a slow habit to build, and I'm nowhere close to finished. But six months into practicing it deliberately, I've noticed the quality of work coming back to me hasn't dropped the way I quietly feared it might. It's just started looking less like a copy of my own instincts and more like the actual judgment of the people I'm supposed to be developing, which was always meant to be the point.

name: Meghan McKenzie
body:
Depending on the season, I'm either on the slopes, on the water, or on the golf course, and for a long time I thought of that as just what I do outside of work, entirely separate from the job, a way to recharge and nothing more than that, no deeper connection worth examining.

I've started to think that's wrong. Fifteen years into a career in enterprise sales, I can trace a surprising amount of how I actually run a growth process back to lessons that came from sport, not from any sales training I ever sat through in a conference room or read about in a book someone handed me early in my career.

Skiing taught me that the fastest way down a slope is rarely the safest one, and that the skiers who genuinely last decades on the mountain, rather than blowing out a knee in their thirties, are the ones who read conditions honestly each run rather than pushing the same aggressive line regardless of what's actually underneath them that particular day. Golf taught me something almost the opposite lesson, and I think the two balance each other out in a useful way: that a single bad hole doesn't have to define the entire round, and that the ability to reset cleanly after a miss is a genuine, trainable skill, not simply a personality trait some people are lucky enough to have been born with and others weren't.

Enterprise sales rewards exactly those two instincts more reliably than almost any "closing technique" I've ever been formally taught in a training session. Reading a deal honestly, on its own terms, instead of forcing whatever approach worked on the last three deals onto a situation that doesn't actually resemble them. Resetting cleanly after a call that didn't go how you wanted or expected, rather than carrying that miss, and the small defensiveness it creates, into the very next conversation with someone who had nothing to do with the last one. I didn't learn either of those instincts from a sales book, however many of those I've read over the years looking for an edge. I learned them on a mountain and a golf course, long before I ever consciously thought to connect the two parts of my life together.

I mention this partly because I think we undersell, in this industry, how much of what actually makes someone good at complex, relationship-heavy sales gets built somewhere other than a CRM or a training deck. The instincts that hold up under real pressure tend to get built slowly, somewhere that has nothing obviously to do with the job, long before anyone thinks to call them a transferable skill.

I try to actually use this when I'm hiring or developing someone on my team now, rather than treating it as a nice reflection to post about. I ask, genuinely, what someone does outside of work that requires patience, honest self-assessment, or the ability to reset after a bad outcome without spiraling, because I've started to trust that answer more than I trust a rehearsed story about a specific deal they closed. The deal story tells me what they want me to think about them. The other answer tends to tell me something closer to how they actually operate when nobody's coaching them through it.

name: Meghan McKenzie
body:
Most growth teams treat mentorship as a nice thing to do for junior people, something separate from the actual work of hitting pipeline numbers, scheduled in when there's time left over rather than budgeted for as part of the job itself. I think that's a mistake, and I'd go further than that: I think mentorship is one of the highest-leverage growth activities on my calendar, not an extracurricular one squeezed in around the edges of the quarter's real priorities.

Here's the honest reasoning behind that, stated as plainly as I can manage it. A sales process that lives only in my head doesn't scale past me, no matter how good that process actually is or how consistently it's produced results over the years. Every hour I spend actually walking someone through why I made a particular call in a deal, not just what I did in the moment but the reasoning sitting underneath it, is an hour that makes the entire team's close rate less dependent on any single person's instincts, including my own, which matters more the larger the team grows.

I've had people tell me, years after we worked together directly, that the thing they remember most isn't a specific deal we closed together, however satisfying that deal might have felt at the time. It's that I treated their development as seriously as I treated the quarter's number, in the actual moment, when it would have been considerably easier and faster to just take the harder calls myself and let them shadow quietly from the sidelines, learning by osmosis rather than by doing.

If you're building a growth team and mentorship keeps getting deprioritized because "there's simply no time this quarter," which is a sentence I've heard from more growth leaders than I can count, I'd push back directly on that framing rather than accepting it as an unavoidable trade-off. The time you don't spend developing your team this quarter is time you'll spend re-explaining the same lessons individually, deal by deal, account by account, for the next several years, because the underlying gap in judgment never actually closes on its own. Mentorship isn't the thing competing with growth for your limited attention. Done properly, and done consistently rather than sporadically when convenient, it's one of the more durable ways you actually get growth in the first place, compounding in a way that a single strong quarter from one person never quite manages to.

I've started building this into how I structure my own week rather than leaving it to whenever a gap happens to appear on the calendar, because gaps like that rarely appear on their own in a growth role. A fixed hour, protected the same way I'd protect time for a client call, spent actually walking through the reasoning behind a deal rather than just the outcome of it. It's a small structural change, and it's made a bigger difference to how quickly people on my team develop real judgment than any single piece of coaching advice I've given in the moment during a live deal.

name: Meghan McKenzie
body:
Before "content marketing" was a category most B2B buyers had a clear name for, I was selling SEO-driven content at Crowd Content, and I want to talk about what that actually required day to day, because selling something the market genuinely doesn't have language for yet is a completely different skill than selling into a category that's already established and understood.

You can't lean on "everyone in your space is already doing this," the single easiest sentence in most B2B sales conversations, when nobody in their space is visibly doing it yet, or at least not doing it in any way a prospect could point to and recognize. Every conversation started from further back than a normal sales call would, first explaining why organic content even mattered to their business at all, before ever getting anywhere close to why our specific approach to producing it was worth paying for over doing it in-house or not doing it at all. It was slower. It required considerably more patience per deal than anything I'd sell later in my career, once the category matured and buyers arrived to a call already half-convinced. But it taught me something I still lean on constantly: to actually diagnose what a buyer believed about their own problem, in their own words, before I ever pitched a specific solution to it.

That skill, sitting patiently with a buyer's actual mental model before trying to sell into it rather than around it, turned out to be far more durable than any pitch deck from that early era, most of which look almost quaint looking back at them now. Categories mature. Language catches up to the reality on the ground. And eventually "content marketing" became a line item every reasonably sophisticated B2B company budgeted for without needing much convincing at all. But the deals I remember most clearly from those genuinely early years weren't won by a sharper pitch or a cleverer deck. They were won by actually understanding what the buyer believed walking into the call, and meeting them there first, before trying to move them anywhere.

I think about this often now, watching a similar pattern play out with GEO and AI visibility. A lot of buyers today are exactly where those early content buyers were: half-aware something has shifted, not yet sure what to call it, and considerably more receptive to someone who starts by understanding their confusion than someone who starts by pitching a solution to a problem they haven't fully named for themselves yet.

It's tempting, watching a new category form in real time, to rush toward the polished pitch as soon as the language starts to stabilize, because a clean pitch feels like progress after years of having to explain the basics on every single call. I'd resist that temptation more than most teams do. The instinct to diagnose before pitching doesn't stop being useful once a category matures; it just becomes easier to skip, because the shorthand starts working often enough that nobody notices how much it's costing them on the calls where the buyer's actual situation doesn't quite match the shorthand.

name: Alicia Braganza
body:
Before I ever worked agency-side, I spent years on the client side, e-commerce, consumer packaged goods, fintech, sitting in the exact seat the people I now manage relationships with are sitting in today, on the receiving end of vendor calls, wondering privately whether the person on the other end actually understood the business or was simply managing the account until the next renewal conversation.

I think that's the single biggest reason my approach to account management looks different from a lot of people who came up purely on the agency side, without ever having sat on the other side of that particular table. I know, from direct lived experience rather than empathy exercises in a training deck, what it actually feels like to be on a call with a vendor who's technically saying all the right things, hitting every expected note, while you privately wonder whether they understand your business at all, or whether you're simply one of forty accounts quietly blurring together for them that particular week.

That client-side time also meant I touched research, product development, content, and SEO directly, hands-on, rather than encountering marketing only in the abstract, filtered through an agency's own internal specialization. When I manage an account now, I'm not translating a client's problem through a purely agency lens built from agency-side experience alone. I'm drawing on what it actually felt like to have that exact problem myself, sitting on the other side of the table, waiting to see whether the partner in front of me would genuinely help or simply manage me politely until the contract came up for renewal.

I don't think agency experience alone teaches you that particular instinct, however many years someone spends doing genuinely excellent agency work. I think you need to have sat in the client's chair at least once, uncomfortable and quietly unsure whether the partner across the table actually understands what you're dealing with, to build the kind of account instincts that don't have to be manually trained in later, because they were formed the hard way the first time, from the wrong side of that particular conversation.

It shows up in small ways more than dramatic ones. I notice myself asking a client, early in a relationship, what their last agency got wrong, not to score points against a predecessor, but because I remember exactly what it felt like to have a complaint that never quite got addressed because nobody on the other side had actually experienced it firsthand.

I also think it's why I've never fully trusted the version of "client-centered" that shows up mostly in pitch decks and onboarding documents. Real client-centeredness, the kind that actually holds up under pressure six months into an engagement, looks less like a stated value and more like a specific, slightly uncomfortable habit: assuming, by default, that the client's frustration is legitimate before assuming it's a misunderstanding on their end, because from the client-side chair, it usually was legitimate, and it usually did take longer to get addressed than it should have.

name: Alicia Braganza
body:
I just wrapped up Profound's AEO Foundation and Analytics certifications, going in with one clear goal I'd set for myself ahead of time: close a specific knowledge gap I knew I had, rather than collect another credential to list somewhere. That gap is genuinely closed now, and I want to share what actually stood out about the experience, because a lot of AEO content circulating online stays frustratingly abstract, long on concepts and short on anything you could actually apply the same week you read it.

The concepts themselves weren't really the hard part, if I'm honest about it. Most of us in this industry have absorbed the broad strokes of how AI answer engines work by now, simply from being around the conversation for the last year or two. What actually moved the needle for me was getting properly hands-on with platform and agent builds and applying them immediately to real client scenarios I was already managing, rather than treating the coursework as theory to revisit "someday" once things settled down, which is exactly the trap I've fallen into with other certifications in the past. Applying it the same week I learned it is what turned the material from information sitting in my notes into an actual working skill I could bring into a client call the following Monday.

The specific shift I'd flag for anyone managing client accounts right now, whether or not you go through this particular certification: it forced me to stop thinking about AEO as a slightly rebranded extension of SEO reporting, tacked onto the same dashboard with a new tab, and start thinking about it as its own genuinely distinct measurement discipline, with its own signals that most existing client reporting infrastructure simply isn't built to surface yet. That's a real, uncomfortable gap between what clients are increasingly asking about in quarterly meetings and what most of our existing tools were designed to track five years ago, and closing that gap properly is going to matter considerably more over the next year than most agencies, ours included until fairly recently, have been treating it.

A big part of credit for how well the cohort landed goes to the instructors who ran it, and I'd genuinely recommend the program to anyone in an account or strategy seat who's been putting off closing this same gap the way I was for longer than I'd like to admit.

What I didn't expect going in was how much value came from being in a cohort at all, rather than working through the material alone. Watching other account and strategy people apply the same concepts to genuinely different client scenarios, a SaaS account here, a manufacturing account there, surfaced edge cases I'd never have thought to ask about on my own, since my own client roster doesn't cover that range. A few of those conversations directly shaped how I explained AEO to one of my own clients the following week, in language clearer than anything I'd have arrived at solo.

If there's one piece of practical advice I'd pass along, it's to go in with a specific, live client scenario already in mind, rather than absorbing the material in the abstract. Having a real account to test each concept against in real time is what turned this from an interesting few days into something I'm already using.

name: Alicia Braganza
body:
A recent anonymous review from one of our higher-ed partners said something I keep coming back to, weeks later: that our team acts as an extension of theirs, bringing subject matter expertise, clear communication, and steady execution across SEO, content strategy, and CRO.

I want to unpack what actually earns a sentence like that, because "we're an extension of your team" is one of those phrases agencies say constantly, in nearly every pitch deck I've ever seen including some of my own early ones, and rarely operationalize into anything a client would actually recognize and repeat back unprompted. For this particular account, it meant showing up to their internal planning conversations already understanding the institutional politics of a higher-ed marketing decision specifically, not just the general SEO mechanics that would apply to any industry. It meant our recommendations referenced their actual enrollment cycles and stakeholder calendar by name, rather than a generic content calendar template lifted from a SaaS playbook and lightly adjusted. And it meant steady execution didn't just mean hitting deadlines reliably, which is table stakes rather than a differentiator at this point. It meant the same handful of people staying consistent on the account long enough that nobody on their side ever had to re-explain context from scratch every quarter to a rotating cast of new faces.

That review followed a documented 40% increase in qualified leads within 90 days for a different account entirely, and I think the two are connected more directly than they might look at first glance, sitting next to each other in a case study deck. The lead increase is the number a case study leads with, because it's clean and quantifiable and looks good on a slide. The "extension of the team" feeling is the actual reason that kind of number tends to be repeatable across quarters, rather than a one-time spike nobody can quite explain or reproduce the following period.

I think about this distinction often when a prospective client asks what makes an engagement with us different from their last agency. The honest answer isn't usually a tactic or a tool, though we have plenty of both. It's closer to what that higher-ed reviewer described: the quiet, cumulative effect of the same people staying present, informed, and genuinely invested long enough that the relationship stops feeling transactional and starts feeling like an actual partnership.

It's also, honestly, the harder thing to sell in a first conversation, because it doesn't reduce cleanly to a bullet point the way "40% increase in qualified leads" does. Prospective clients want proof, reasonably, and a number is the fastest proof available. But I've started trying to pair every number we share with the specific, less quantifiable habit that produced it, because I think clients who've been burned by an agency before are listening for exactly that pairing, whether or not they'd phrase it that way themselves.

name: Khaled Fouly
body:
I don't usually bet on outcomes with clients, but I gave one client a genuine double-or-nothing offer once, and I think the story is worth telling in full, because of how it actually turned around in the room rather than how it looks summarized in a single sentence afterward.

Their business ran almost entirely on paid media, with close to no organic traffic to fall back on if the ad account ever slowed down. Site performance scored a 2 out of 100 on any standard test you'd care to run. Code bloat everywhere, the kind that accumulates over years of nobody being assigned to own it. The experience was, by any honest measure, rough for a visitor trying to actually convert. My point of contact told me upfront, before we ever got in the room together, that the CEO probably wasn't going to buy into anything we proposed, she believed we could still shift the account's trajectory, but she was managing my expectations carefully, the way someone does when they've sat through this exact meeting failing before. What made it harder still: the team had already quietly convinced themselves they'd maxed out how much they could optimize paid search, and had shifted their attention instead toward social, photo and film shoots, and other efforts, treating the ad account itself as something to simply let the algorithms run without much further intervention.

The pitch started exactly how you'd expect, given all of that context walking in. The CEO was visibly checked out within the first few minutes, doing that specific thing people do in meetings where they're clearly present in the room but have already mentally filed the conversation as a formality. So we changed tactics entirely, on the spot, rather than pushing forward with the deck as planned, instead of talking about campaigns and creative, we talked about the actual levers underneath paid performance that nobody in that room had ever connected directly to their ad results: site speed, SEO foundations, Google Analytics hygiene, first-party data quality. I watched him start to lean back into the conversation, physically shift posture, and for a moment I genuinely wasn't sure whether it was real interest or just him working out how to end the meeting politely without seeming rude about it.

It was real interest. And the lesson I keep coming back to, months later, whenever a new account looks similarly stuck: when paid performance genuinely stalls despite reasonable effort, the instinct is almost always to look inside the ad account itself for the fix, adjusting bids and creative and targeting. Most of the time, in my experience, the actual problem is sitting one layer beneath that, in places nobody in the room has ever been trained to look, and the account only starts moving again once someone's willing to say so plainly, in a room where the easier, more comfortable thing to do would have been to just talk about the ad account like everyone expected.

name: Khaled Fouly
body:
Paid media often gets pulled into a growth strategy far too early, and I think it's one of the most expensive mistakes a growth team can make, repeated often enough across enough companies that I've stopped thinking of it as an occasional misjudgment: using paid spend to hunt for your ICP or prove product-market fit before either of those things actually exists yet.

That's not what paid media is designed to do, however much pressure teams instinctively put on it to do exactly that, usually because a working paid channel feels like the fastest available lever when growth has stalled and everyone's looking for something to point to. It's expected, constantly and unreasonably, to somehow identify the ideal customer, test messaging, and validate product-market fit, all at once, under a single monthly budget that was never sized for that many open questions simultaneously.
