Paid was never built for that job, and treating it as though it could do that job is where I've watched more budgets quietly disappear than almost any other single mistake in this industry. Paid is a multiplier. It takes whatever is already resonating with a real, validated audience and makes it bigger, faster, more visible than it would ever become organically on its own. It also takes whatever isn't resonating yet and burns through budget exposing that fact just as efficiently and just as fast, which is the part nobody wants to hear in the meeting where the spend gets approved.

When the underlying strategy is genuinely clear, you actually know your ICP, and your messaging has already been tested somewhere considerably cheaper than a live ad account, whether that's cold outreach, a landing page test, or direct conversations with real prospects, paid accelerates real, already-existing momentum. When that clarity isn't there yet, paid doesn't surface the gap gently or cheaply. It just accelerates the spend while the underlying uncertainty about who you're actually talking to stays exactly as unresolved as it was before the campaign ever launched, just considerably more expensive to keep not-knowing.

If your paid results feel inconsistent in a way nobody on the team can quite explain, month over month, despite reasonable optimization effort, I'd ask a different, more uncomfortable question before touching the ad account itself again: has messaging actually been validated somewhere, with someone, in a real conversation, before it ever reached a paid channel at all? More often than most teams expect when I ask this directly, the honest answer is no, and no amount of further campaign optimization fixes a problem that was never actually a campaign problem to begin with, no matter how many hours get spent adjusting bids and creative in search of a fix that isn't there.

The uncomfortable follow-up question, once a team admits that gap out loud, is usually whether they're willing to slow the paid spend down while the validation work actually happens elsewhere. Most teams say yes in principle and then quietly keep the ad account running at full speed anyway, because pausing spend feels like losing momentum even when the spend was never actually generating the kind of signal they needed.

name: Khaled Fouly
body:
I charge clients a flat, previously agreed fee that doesn't change unless the actual scope of work changes drastically, not a commission calculated on ad spend. I want to explain why in some detail, because it's a genuinely different economic relationship than most paid media agencies offer their clients, and the difference matters considerably more than it sounds when it's stated as a single line in a pricing page.

Commission-based paid media pricing creates a quiet, structural incentive problem that most people in the industry don't discuss openly, even though almost everyone in it privately understands it exists: the agency earns more, directly and mechanically, when the client spends more, entirely regardless of whether spending more is actually the right call for that account in that particular month. I don't think most agencies running commission models are acting in obvious bad faith about this, deliberately inflating spend they know is wasteful. I think the incentive simply sits there in the background, shaping small decisions nobody has to consciously choose for it to matter, the way any misaligned incentive tends to quietly bend behavior over time without anyone involved feeling like they've done anything wrong.

A flat fee removes that incentive from the relationship entirely, cleanly, rather than trying to manage around it with disclosures or good intentions. If I recommend pulling back spend on an underperforming channel, that recommendation isn't in any tension with my own revenue that month, which means a client never has to sit there wondering whether my advice is actually about their business or quietly, half-consciously, about my own commission for the quarter. That single removed doubt changes the texture of nearly every strategic conversation we have afterward.

It costs me something real in the months a client scales spend significantly and I'm not capturing any percentage of that growth, which is worth being honest about rather than pretending the flat-fee model is costless for me. I've made genuine peace with that trade, because the trust it buys compounds steadily over the life of the relationship in a way a single bigger commission check never would, quarter to quarter. Clients on this model tend to stay considerably longer than industry averages I've seen elsewhere, push back less defensively when I recommend cutting something that isn't working, and treat me less like a vendor managing their budget on their behalf and more like someone actually managing their outcome alongside them, which was always the relationship I wanted to be in, long before I ever structured the pricing to match it.

I get asked, fairly often, whether this model is simply harder to sell, since most prospective clients have never been offered it before and don't immediately have language for why it's better for them. It is a slightly harder pitch upfront, and I've stopped trying to shorten that conversation just to close faster, because the clients who take the time to actually understand why the incentive structure matters tend to be exactly the ones who stay long enough for the model to prove itself.

Business owners selling complex services or products often limit their growth when they mistake a single social platform for the entire buyer journey, rather than recognising it as one intentional component within a broader commercial system. Most do not realise the cost of that misunderstanding until pipeline momentum has slowed.

The recurring debate over whether LinkedIn, Instagram, Substack, or X is the 'best' platform misses the point entirely. Each can contribute to visibility and credibility. None, in isolation, constitutes a buyer journey.

One of the most common mistakes in B2B markets is optimising content for feed performance rather than buyer progression. These are fundamentally different objectives.

The more important discipline is signal interpretation.

Customer feedback, platform analytics, and market response are valuable inputs only when examined critically. Not every signal carries equal weight.

A focused, intentional channel mix, selected for its ability to influence the right stakeholders at the right stage of the buying process, will consistently outperform a broad but reactive presence.

Social media should function as a signal layer.

The conversion engine itself should be built elsewhere: through credible proof, substantive conversations, institutional trust, and a buying experience designed for considered decisions rather than momentary attention.

Every time a B2B brand captures disproportionate market attention, commentary follows almost immediately.

Within 48 hours, the post-analysis begins.

The algorithm favored it. The timing aligned with distribution windows. The format reflected an emerging content pattern.

Each explanation is technically reasonable, but none of them is strategically instructive.

The more consequential variable is the ex-ante strategic thesis.

Why that positioning? Why that buyer persona? Why that framing? Why that timing?

This is where durable B2B marketing advantage actually resides: in pre-outcome strategic reasoning.

Before performance dashboards validate the decision, a strategist must determine which hypothesis deserves commitment.

If a marketing organization proceeds to execution without establishing this ex-ante strategic thesis, it is effectively deploying capital and creative assets without directional conviction.

If we are pursuing non-linear enterprise impact, the standard of thinking that precedes execution must also rise.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
What many founders (or marketing agencies) overlook is a foundational principle: before attempting to capture the attention of your target audience with a worn, manipulative hook, you must first establish alignment.

In practical terms, you must operate on the same wavelength as the person you intend to reach.

Association does the substantive work.

Every subject line, message, and campaign either strengthens the right associations or quietly erodes them.

Whether an email is opened or someone clicks 'see more' is secondary.

The more consequential question is one of strategic coherence.

If the majority of your audience does not experience your framing as intelligent, relevant, and contextually appropriate, you are effectively borrowing attention at the expense of brand equity.

Short-term curiosity is a fragile return.

The long-term cost is dilution of the associations that position you as credible, deliberate, and worth engaging.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
The prevailing advice on LinkedIn urges founders to build a founder-led brand.

The underlying observations are correct. The strategic conclusion most people draw from them is not.

When every post casts you as the hero, the prospect becomes a spectator.

In any effective narrative, there is only one hero.

If your objective is to move a prospect closer to a buying decision, that hero cannot be you. It must be them.

A founder-as-hero narrative becomes a profile piece.

A customer-as-hero narrative begins with the reader's problem, articulates the tension, and provides a framework for making a better decision.

You do not disappear. You shift from protagonist to guide.

You are not the one on the quest; you are the one with the map.

This positioning decision reshapes everything downstream.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
Last month, I reviewed the LinkedIn communication of a company that had published more than a hundred posts over six months.

Individually, many were insightful.

Yet despite the volume and quality, the communication failed to create meaningful influence.

Each post subtly positioned the company in a different mental category.

Every interaction with a prospect is a micro-commitment.

For that commitment to compound, two things must happen.

First, the reader must conclude: 'This is valuable.'

Second, they must give you permission to return.

Repetition, when coherent, creates structure.

Authority is simply the byproduct of consistently placing aligned signals into the same cognitive frame.

The common mistake is placing bricks into different buildings.

When a prospect lands on your profile, they should immediately associate you with one clear idea.

That is how positioning compounds over time.

name: Suvam Sahoo
body:
Over time, my understanding of what it truly means to build a company has changed completely.

Most people know me as someone who loves the process, the thrill of building and operating companies.

What fewer people know is that my philosophy around building has evolved dramatically.

There’s a saying I’ve come to believe:

"Busy founders are seldom great. Great founders are seldom busy."

And that evolution continues to shape how I build Knox today.

I once believed the founder was the company, the person who had to push hardest, hustle longest, and stay busiest.

But hard work, I’ve learned, is a function of both effort and value.

Effort is finite; it’s constrained by time.

Value, on the other hand, can expand infinitely when leveraged through systems and people.

In the early days, every founder does it all. You write the code, close the deals, fix the bugs, and take out the trash. It’s a necessary phase, but not a scalable one.

The pivotal shift happens when you hire people who are better than you at their craft, and then give them the trust and ownership to lead.

Because the true job of a CEO isn’t to do everything; it’s to make themselves increasingly replaceable. To continuously step out of roles and elevate their focus to the next level.

If your company needs you to function every day, then it stops when you do.

name: Suvam Sahoo
body:
Finding the right Shopify expert in India is not about availability. There is no shortage of talent. What there is, is a shortage of informed decisions.

Most businesses follow a familiar pattern: they post "Looking for a Shopify developer," receive dozens of responses, select the most confident candidate, and find themselves reassessing the decision a few months later when delivery falls short of expectations.

But the real issue is a lack of clarity around requirements.

Shopify is not a single discipline. The term "Shopify expert" is often too broad to be useful.

Here is my take on who to bring in based on your current stage and growth plans:

(1) Freelancers

Pros:
- Lower cost with flexible engagement terms
- Fast to onboard for short, well-scoped projects
- Direct communication with the person doing the work
- Wide availability across skill sets and budgets

Cons:
- Single point of failure
- Limited capacity for large projects
- No built-in project management or QA process
- Continuity risk on longer engagements

(2) Shopify Agencies

Pros:
- Dedicated team across design, development, QA, and strategy
- Better accountability and scalability
- Structured project delivery

Cons:
- Higher cost
- Quality varies significantly
- Some agencies rely on inexperienced resources

(3) In-House Developers

Pros:
- Deep understanding of your business
- Fast turnaround
- Long-term alignment
- Cost-efficient at scale

Cons:
- High ownership cost
- Hiring takes time
- Knowledge concentration risk
- Best suited for brands with ongoing development needs

Refer back to this before your next Shopify hiring decision.

name: Suvam Sahoo

A question I hear very frequently from founders is:

"With so many tools and plugins available, what should be integrated from day one and what can wait?"

The answer is simpler than most expect.

In the early stages, your objective is not to build the most feature-rich storefront. Your objective is to create a buying experience that is clear, credible, and frictionless.

Founders often mistake app installations for progress.

What is essential from day one?

(1) Reliable payment infrastructure.

(2) Shipping and post-purchase communication.

(3) Foundational analytics.

A few things to avoid:

(i) Don't adopt an app-first mindset.

(ii) Don't scale features before demand.

(iii) Don't build based on assumptions.

The most effective ecommerce operators build for the customers they have today.

Remember: Master the basics. Complexity takes care of itself.

name: Suvam Sahoo

India’s D2C market is growing very fast. Every month, many new brands are launched.

But when you look closely, a different picture appears.

Many new brands fail because they never find product-market fit.

One of the biggest mistakes founders make is believing India is one single market.

It is not.

India is made up of many different customer groups with different cultures, buying habits, price expectations, and preferences.

Another major problem is that too many brands are copying each other.

Most are selling similar products, using similar marketing, and targeting customers in the same way.

Before starting another brand in an already crowded category, founders should ask one important question:

What real customer problem still needs to be solved, and can we solve it better than others?

That is what strong positioning really means.

There are still hundreds of consumer problems waiting to be solved better.

That is what I hope to see more of in the years ahead: Indian brands growing into globally respected consumer companies.

If you run a B2B or SaaS business, you already know that security is no longer a background concern. It influences how enterprise buyers decide which vendors they will trust with their data, workflows, and customers.

Many cybersecurity firms still operate using a model that feels out of step with modern product teams.

A traditional security assessment often takes six or seven days. Developers then spend several more days implementing fixes, followed by another verification cycle.

By the time that loop closes, ten to fourteen days have passed, and the team still lacks continuous visibility into its real risk surface.

At Brahm Security, we built a system that reports vulnerabilities in real time.

This gives engineering teams live visibility as issues emerge, making it easier to understand their impact and resolve them within the same workflow where code is already being shipped.

Both my co-founder and I stay closely involved throughout the engagement.

We work with teams that understand how software ships, how engineering organizations operate, and how technical risk translates into business impact.

Security that is measurable, continuous, and integrated should become both a trust signal and a commercial advantage.

If you want to treat security as a continuous practice instead of a one-time compliance exercise, this is the kind of process worth looking for.

name: Darpan Vashi
body:
"We understand the importance of security, but it does not fit within our current budget."

This is a familiar response from founders and technology leaders.

It reflects a persistent misconception that cybersecurity is a discretionary expense rather than a core business function.

Cybersecurity rarely generates revenue directly. Its value lies in protecting continuity, trust, and enterprise value.

Modern attackers increasingly rely on automation and AI to identify the easiest targets, and those targets are often smaller organizations.

The resistance typically appears across three dimensions:

(1) Financial: Security competes with growth initiatives.

(2) Operational: Organizations rely on outdated controls while overestimating the friction of modern security practices.

(3) Psychological: Many assume that because nothing has happened yet, nothing will happen in the future.

That assumption is becoming increasingly dangerous.

Regulations are tightening, cyber insurance requirements are increasing, and executive accountability continues to expand.

The question is no longer whether cybersecurity is expensive.

The question is whether your organization can absorb the compounded cost of inaction.

Security should be integrated into the operating model, continuously managed, routinely tested, and aligned with business objectives.

name: Darpan Vashi
body:
Security leaders are constantly told to automate more.

Deploy another platform. Integrate another system. Reduce response times.

Yet despite all this activity, outcomes often remain unchanged.

The problem is not the absence of automation.

The problem is treating automation as a tooling upgrade instead of an operating model.

If you are responsible for security, the real question is not whether to automate, but what you are asking automation to execute.

Automation only works when governance already exists.

Without clearly defined ownership, decision rights, and operating boundaries, automation simply accelerates disorder.

Define what must never happen inside your environment.

Establish control boundaries based on business risk.

Only then should automation enforce those decisions consistently at machine speed.

The organizations that stand out will not be those that merely adopt AI or automation.

They will be the ones that apply it intentionally, anchored in governance and trusted because it behaves consistently.

Everything else is simply faster marketing noise.

name: Darpan Vashi

I have spent over five years in cybersecurity.

Early in my career, my thinking revolved around controls, frameworks, and compliance checklists.

That perspective changed when I began working directly with enterprise executives.

Executives do not think in terms of controls.

They think in outcomes, trade-offs, resilience, and organizational survival.

One conversation with an executive exposed a major blind spot in how I communicated the value of security.

The most important lesson I have learned is that meaningful cybersecurity begins when technical concepts are translated into business language.

Security is not simply about deploying policies.

It is about aligning strategy with business priorities and balancing speed with resilience.

Some organizations prioritize growth. Others prioritize stability.

Cybersecurity is not only technical.

It is strategic, contextual, and inseparable from leadership's long-term vision.

name: Yash T
body:
We are only two years into the commercialization of generative AI, yet its trajectory is already reshaping how modern enterprises operate.

What began as a tool to enhance productivity is rapidly becoming the architecture upon which businesses are built.

AI is emerging as the operational core of applications across the stack, from frontend interfaces to backend infrastructure and everything in between.

Based on extensive conversations with enterprise leadership teams over the past six months, three structural shifts are becoming increasingly clear.

__________

1. Agentic AI Will Redefine Enterprise Workflows

Enterprises are beginning to deploy AI not as isolated tools but as networks of autonomous agents capable of reasoning, planning, and acting.

These agents will increasingly:
• Design and execute complex workflows
• Improve outputs through iterative self-correction
• Collaborate with both human teams and other AI systems

Generative AI is also dismantling longstanding organizational constraints.

Silos are weakening as access to powerful AI tools becomes more broadly distributed, enabling cross-functional collaboration and accelerating innovation.

__________

2. Multimodal AI Will Become the Default Standard

The next wave of enterprise AI will be fundamentally multimodal.

Systems capable of understanding text, images, video, audio, and code together will become the default.

For organizations, this enables:
• Richer contextual understanding
• Smarter, more responsive systems
• Personalized customer experiences at scale

Multimodality moves AI closer to how humans process information, dramatically expanding its enterprise applications.

__________

3. The Industry Is Entering the Era of AI Optimization

If the past two years were defined by experimentation, the next phase will be defined by optimization.

Organizations are moving beyond pilots toward disciplined deployment and measurable business outcomes.

• More than 70% of organizations are already reporting positive ROI from generative AI initiatives.
• Continued optimization and declining compute costs will unlock an even broader range of enterprise use cases.

This reflects Jevons’ Paradox: as efficiency improves and costs decline, overall usage expands.

Looking ahead, AI development will likely follow two complementary paths:

i) Massive frontier models designed for complex reasoning.

ii) Smaller, specialized models optimized for edge devices.

Together, these trends will make AI both more powerful and more ubiquitous across every layer of enterprise technology.

name: Yash T
body:
Across the APAC region, businesses are deploying generative AI at a pace roughly 30% faster than their counterparts in more developed markets.

A major driver behind this acceleration is a highly digital-native workforce that is comfortable experimenting with emerging technologies.

Yet speed of adoption does not necessarily translate into realized value.

Despite increasing employee usage, many organizations remain far from capturing the full return on their AI investments.

Current data suggests that only about half of surveyed employees meaningfully use generative AI in their daily work.

Even more revealing, among Searce's 200+ customers across Southeast Asia, only around 5% have successfully moved these capabilities into full production environments.

This highlights a widening execution gap.

Organizations are enthusiastic about AI adoption, but enthusiasm alone is not a strategy.

Without clear governance, operational integration, and leadership alignment, generative AI risks remaining an experimental layer instead of becoming a transformative capability.

The imperative is not simply to introduce AI tools.

It is to redesign how work gets done.

Leaders must embed AI into core workflows while rethinking existing processes to leverage the scale and speed AI introduces.

Done correctly, this creates three measurable outcomes:

• Revenue expansion through new products, services, and capabilities.
• Lower operating costs through intelligent automation.
• Continuous innovation that strengthens long-term competitiveness.

For organizations across APAC, AI should no longer be treated as a novelty.

It should be treated as a strategic capability embedded across the enterprise.

That requires sustained investment in workforce capability, technical fluency, and responsible deployment.

Organizations that make this commitment will benefit from higher productivity, faster innovation cycles, and a durable competitive advantage in an increasingly AI-driven economy.

name: Micaela
body:
I’m the founder of Inizia. Over the years, I’ve often been asked a deceptively simple question: what does the name actually signify?

When I began formalizing the company, I knew the name could not be ornamental. It needed to reflect a point of view: how we think about technology and how we approach building products.

I was drawn to Latin, a language that underpins many modern languages, much like technology underpins today's economies.

During that exploration, I discovered *Inizio*, meaning "to begin." It felt directionally right, but incomplete.

As a woman building in technology, I wanted that perspective embedded into the identity itself, so replacing the final "o" with an "a" became a deliberate act of authorship.

*Inizio* became *Inizia*.

What followed added another layer of meaning. In Italian, "Inizia" is imperative.

Begin.

That single word captures how we approach our work.

We partner with founders at the point where ideas must become execution.

Our role is to:

• Introduce clarity
• Create structure
• Build products designed to endure, not merely function

Our work is guided by a few principles:

• Designing scalable web and mobile products with usability and long-term performance in mind
• Operating as a focused, high-agency team that owns the product lifecycle end to end
• Partnering closely with early-stage and growth companies to transform ambition into reliable systems

We are intentional about what we build, and equally intentional about how we build it.

I'm grateful to every founder and team who trusts us with that responsibility.

name: Micaela
body:
The term "Product Manager" has become one of the most common titles in technology, yet one of the least consistently understood.

At its highest standard, a product manager is not a coordinator of process, but a steward of outcomes.

The role exists to answer a far more important question than "Did we ship?"

It asks:

"Are we solving the right problem?"

Many organizations reduce product management to maintaining roadmaps, running ceremonies, and managing backlogs.

I think of this as the appearance of product management without its substance.

This reveals a deeper tension inside product organizations:

(1) The output mindset values speed, consistency, and delivery.

(2) The outcome mindset values customer understanding, validation, and solving meaningful problems.

Neither perspective is wrong.

The more useful question is: which capability is currently missing?

Many teams execute exceptionally well while remaining strategically underpowered.

They manage delivery but lack ownership of the underlying problem space.

That is why outcome-oriented product leadership matters.

Not because execution is unimportant, but because flawless execution against the wrong premise is still failure.

Likewise, product thinking without shipped value remains incomplete.

The standard is not choosing between thinking and shipping.

It is integrating both with discipline.

name: Micaela
body:
When I began my career as a developer, I believed writing more code meant creating more value.

Experience taught me otherwise.

No framework, programming language, or perfectly structured repository can compensate for solving the wrong problem.

Today, writing software has become increasingly accessible.

Deciding what is worth building has become the real differentiator.

The most valuable developers are not simply those who complete tasks.

They understand the problem, design thoughtful solutions, and use the right tools, including AI, with speed and precision.

From working with developers and engineering teams, a few principles consistently stand out:

1. Think about problems before implementation.

2. Use AI as a multiplier, not a substitute for judgment.

3. Optimize for delivery instead of perfection.

4. Learn enduring principles like systems thinking and architecture rather than chasing frameworks.

5. Demonstrate ownership by questioning assumptions and improving decisions.

The common thread is simple.

Clarity of thought consistently outperforms sheer output.

Developers who cultivate judgment will remain valuable regardless of how technology evolves.

name: Micaela
body:
If your product feels somewhat unrefined immediately after launch, that is often evidence of a disciplined product approach.

Many teams believe products should feel complete before release.

In reality, the first version should focus on delivering the core value through the happy path.

Edge cases, operational constraints, and experience refinements only become visible through real-world usage.

I often compare this to architecture.

A building reveals its strengths and weaknesses only after people begin using it.

Products behave the same way.

A launch is not the finish line.

It is the moment the doors open.

Real usage replaces assumptions.

Patterns emerge.

Friction becomes visible.

Priorities become clearer.

The challenge is not responding to every piece of feedback.

The challenge is distinguishing signal from noise.

Products that endure are not those that launch perfectly.

They are the ones that evolve deliberately through disciplined iteration informed by actual customer behavior.

name: Micaela
body:
Some of the strongest technology outcomes I have witnessed emerge when founders and product teams operate as disciplined partners rather than in isolation.

Founders bring deep understanding of the market, customers, and the problem worth solving.

Product teams transform that context into scalable systems.

That responsibility extends well beyond delivery.

It includes product architecture, MVP strategy, UI/UX direction, feature prioritization, and often evolves into fractional CTO leadership.

When product teams operate without sustained founder involvement, familiar problems appear:

• Misaligned assumptions
• Product drift
• Rising costs
• Slower validation cycles

The strongest products emerge when both sides remain actively engaged.

Founders continuously refine the problem space through customer insight.

Product teams challenge assumptions, extract structure from ambiguity, and translate domain expertise into thoughtful technical execution.

When that partnership exists, the result is more than a product.

It becomes a system grounded in market reality, designed to evolve, and built to scale.

name: Kirt
body:
For much of my career, I believed the late-1990s internet boom was a once-in-a-generation transformation. In hindsight, it was only the beginning.

What we are witnessing today with artificial intelligence will surpass it by an order of magnitude.

Over the coming years, the pace and scale of technological advancement will accelerate dramatically.

This is not simply another innovation cycle. It is a structural shift in how industries operate, make decisions, and create value.

Artificial intelligence has already begun reshaping multiple industries, although adoption remains uneven.

The organizations that recognize its operational potential early will define the standards of the next decade.

At Company Name, our focus is clear: delivering specialized technology solutions that strengthen connectivity and digital infrastructure across the hospitality industry.

We help hotels improve operational capability while delivering seamless, high-performance Wi-Fi experiences that meet modern guest expectations.

Today, most hospitality technology projects move through three core stages:

1. Procurement
2. Quoting
3. Stationing and deployment

Historically, each stage has required significant manual coordination.

Artificial intelligence is now beginning to automate, optimize, and accelerate these workflows, unlocking efficiencies that were previously difficult to achieve.

Our objective is not simply to adopt these technologies, but to lead their implementation across hospitality.

The work is technically demanding, but the direction is unmistakable.

AI-enabled infrastructure and operations will become the industry standard.

We are only at the beginning of that transformation.

name: Kirt
body:
Selecting the right ISP or technology partner has always been an important decision for hotels. The answer, however, is more nuanced than many expect.

A strong partner is not simply a provider of connectivity.

It is an organization that understands:

• What is being delivered
• Why it matters
• How it must be implemented within the operational realities of hospitality

Most importantly, they must possess a genuine understanding of the hotel industry.

Hospitality is fundamentally different from a typical enterprise environment.

Guest expectations, operational continuity, and service reliability operate on an entirely different standard.

So who truly fulfills that role?

After more than two decades observing this industry, one conclusion has become increasingly clear.

The concept of the "ideal ISP" for hotels does not truly exist.

Not because capable providers are unavailable, but because the structure of the industry itself has evolved.

Most Internet Service Providers no longer maintain hospitality-focused divisions.

Instead, they rely on channel ecosystems, resellers, system integrators, and intermediaries to serve specialized industries.

Hotels have become one customer segment among many.

This shift is neither good nor bad.

It simply reflects how technology services are now delivered.

But it also reveals an important reality.

The traditional vision of one perfectly aligned ISP partner is largely a myth.

If such a partner is to emerge again, it will require a different type of company—one purpose-built to bridge the gap between infrastructure providers and the operational needs of hospitality.

In many ways, that intermediary layer is already shaping the future of the industry.

name: Alex F
role: Co-Founder | Investor | Top Clay.com Enterprise Partner
body:
When Ali and I started Understory, the conventional wisdom was that a growth agency should specialize narrowly because clients supposedly wanted a vendor who did one thing exceptionally well rather than several things adequately.

For a long time, I believed that too.

But after spending enough time inside B2B technology companies, I noticed something the specialization argument conveniently ignored.

The channels were never actually separate in practice.

Paid social, outbound, executive content, and RevOps were all influencing the same audience, generating the same buying signals, and ultimately contributing to the same revenue outcomes.

I remember sitting in a client meeting where three different vendors each explained the same quarter's pipeline from completely different perspectives.

Each quietly claimed credit for the same handful of deals.

Nobody in the room—including the client—could confidently explain which channel had actually moved the prospect.

That wasn't a reporting problem.

It was a systems problem.

Specialization had been mistaken for rigor.

Instead of building another agency responsible for one slice of go-to-market, we built Understory around one integrated operating model.

One team.
One dataset.
One shared set of buyer signals.

An outbound reply informs paid media.
Executive content sharpens targeting.
Clay workflows identify buying intent across the system.

It sounds obvious.

Yet very few agencies are built this way because integration demands accountability.

Four and a half years later, after becoming one of Clay's leading enterprise partners globally and growing to nearly thirty people, one lesson continues to stand out.

Revenue per employee—not leads or impressions—is the metric worth optimizing.

A GTM system that makes your existing team dramatically more productive creates far more value than disconnected vendors ever can.

That gap—not any single tactic—is what ultimately built Understory.

name: Alex F
role: Co-Founder | Investor | Top Clay.com Enterprise Partner
body:
One of the most common disappointments I see happens roughly six weeks after a company implements Clay.

The problem usually isn't Clay itself.

The problem is that organizations expect a tool and end up needing an operating system.

The pattern is remarkably consistent.

Someone sees a demo, builds an enrichment workflow, replaces manual research, and initially sees strong results.

Then performance plateaus.

Sequences become generic.

Reply rates flatten.

Eventually people conclude Clay was overhyped.

In reality, they built a workflow instead of building a system.

Systems evolve.

Workflows decay.

The companies that extract long-term value from Clay consistently do three things well.

• They design enrichment waterfalls intentionally, prioritizing reliable and cost-efficient data sources before expensive fallback providers.

• They build targeting around buying signals—leadership changes, hiring activity, technology migrations—instead of generic firmographics every competitor uses.

• They continuously refine outbound using real reply data rather than assuming the first workflow will remain effective forever.

This has very little to do with Clay itself.

It is about understanding GTM engineering.

The objective isn't automation for its own sake.

The objective is systematically removing manual work while continuously improving decisions tied directly to business outcomes.

The agencies that understand this distinction are usually the ones whose clients continue expanding their Clay implementation long after the original engagement ends.

name: Alex F
role: Co-Founder | Investor | Top Clay.com Enterprise Partner
body:
Many organizations purchase RevOps expecting a strategic revenue function.

What they often receive is outsourced CRM administration.

Those are fundamentally different services.

Real Revenue Operations isn't about maintaining dashboards or cleaning Salesforce records.

It exists to understand where revenue leaks across marketing, sales, and customer success—and to fix those leaks.

The uncomfortable question RevOps should always answer is:

Where exactly is revenue being lost between stages, and who owns solving it?

Too many companies buy another attribution platform before spending a single afternoon honestly mapping what happens to a lead during the first forty-eight hours after conversion.

Technology rarely fixes process confusion.

It often hides it.

That's why our RevOps function sits inside the same operating model as paid media, outbound, content, and GTM engineering.

Attribution only becomes meaningful when one team can trace an account from first impression through closed revenue.

If your RevOps engagement begins by discussing software configuration instead of revenue movement, you're probably buying operational support packaged as strategic transformation.

Eventually, the dashboards become cleaner.

But revenue barely changes.

name: Alex F
role: Co-Founder | Investor | Top Clay.com Enterprise Partner
body:
One prospective client agreed to meet largely out of courtesy.

They were already working with another paid media agency and had no immediate intention of switching.

Most agencies respond by pitching harder.

We did the opposite.

Before the call, we audited the account using publicly available information and whatever data the prospect was willing to share.

Instead of generic best practices, we highlighted specific opportunities.

• Audience segments that had gone stale.
• Creative that had clearly passed peak performance.
• Budget allocation decisions quietly working against each other.

The purpose wasn't to criticize the incumbent agency.

It was to demonstrate understanding.

Specificity builds trust.

Generic recommendations rarely do.

The client hired us for paid social and paid search before we even submitted a formal proposal.

Not because we made bigger promises.

Because we demonstrated deeper understanding.

Today that's become policy.

We'd rather identify five meaningful issues unique to your business than provide fifty recommendations that could apply to almost anyone.

Trust comes from relevance—not volume.

name: Alex F
role: Co-Founder | Investor | Top Clay.com Enterprise Partner
body:
Executive content on LinkedIn usually falls into one of two categories.

It either becomes a genuine growth lever.

Or it becomes expensive theatre.

Most organizations are unknowingly funding the second.

The theatre version is easy to recognize.

Safe opinions.
Well-formatted posts.
Predictable engagement from colleagues.

By next week, nobody outside the company remembers it existed.

The version that actually builds pipeline requires something much harder.

A real point of view.

Something specific enough that competitors may disagree with it.

Thought leadership has never been about avoiding disagreement.

It has always been about making a defensible argument.

Specificity is difficult to fake.

Buyers recognize that.

Across our B2B technology clients, we've consistently seen the same pattern.

Executives who commit to a genuine perspective become trusted voices whose content directly supports pipeline.

Those who remain safely generic continue collecting engagement without influencing buying decisions.

That's why executive content sits upstream of every other GTM motion we run.

Strong content doesn't just build reputation.

It generates signals.

The accounts engaging with meaningful opinions reveal exactly who is paying attention.

Viewed this way, executive content stops being a branding exercise.

It becomes one of the most efficient signal-generation channels inside a modern GTM system.

name: Medha Thakkar
body:
I don't want to work like a man anymore.

Does that sound confusing? Especially in a world where women are constantly striving to match or surpass men in the workplace?

Let me explain.

I want to grow every year. I want to earn more. I want to challenge myself and succeed in everything I do—but not by running a race that was never designed for me. Not by following an aggressive, relentless standard of work set by someone else.

My benchmark is myself. My pace is my own.

I want to work in a way that is gentle yet powerful, kind yet ambitious. I want to focus on meaningful connections—with inspiring people and with myself. I want success, but not at the cost of burnout.

After much reflection, here's my plan:

• Focusing on health—nourishing my body in a sustainable way, beyond crash diets and misinformation.

• Working on projects that help me evolve—not just working because I must, but because it aligns with my bigger purpose.

• Being an explorer—seeking new perspectives, places, communities, and experiences that fuel my growth.

On this Women's Day, I choose to embrace the rhythm of a woman—one that is intuitive, cyclical, deeply connected, and self-driven.

I don't want to work like a man.

I want to work like me.

name: Medha Thakkar
body:
Over the past 1.5 years, I've organized more than 30 events, and each one has taught me something different.

One pattern, however, has remained surprisingly consistent.

1. Most people register at the last minute.

Roughly 60% of attendees sign up on the day of the event.

I've experienced events with only one registration the night before that ended up selling out within hours.

It taught me an important lesson.

Instead of panicking, prepare.

• Arrange extra chairs and refreshments.
• Keep backup materials ready.
• Brief your team and vendors clearly.
• And remind yourself that patience beats panic.

2. Be honest with speakers and partners.

Community events are naturally unpredictable.

So today I simply tell speakers:

"It might be five people or two hundred—but they'll be the right people."

Most appreciate the honesty.

Some of the most meaningful conversations I've witnessed happened in rooms with fewer than ten people.

If you're organizing an event and feeling uncertain, you're not alone.

Every event teaches you something new.

I'm still learning too.

name: Medha Thakkar
body:
After organizing more than 30 events over the past 1.5 years, one lesson continues to stand out.

People rarely remember every presentation.

They remember how the event made them feel.

Comfort creates connection.

When people feel relaxed, they participate more openly, build stronger relationships, and leave with experiences they'll actually remember.

Some of the small things that consistently help:

Before the event:
• Send one or two friendly reminders.
• Keep the tone conversational rather than formal.

During the event:
• Welcome people warmly.
• Offer a simple drink.
• Use comfortable seating, soft lighting, and calm music.
• Always have a few questions ready in case conversations slow down.

After the event:
• Send a thank-you message.
• Share photos—people genuinely enjoy seeing themselves and celebrating the experience.

These details seem small individually.

Together, they're often why people return.

name: Medha Thakkar
body:
I was a commerce student.

Today, I'm Head of Marketing.

Looking back, the journey has been anything but linear.

I graduated with a B.Com degree and qualified as an ACCA affiliate.

I explored public policy, interned with the Reserve Bank of India, studied in Singapore, worked with purpose-driven consumer brands, spent time in Paris focusing on innovation, started my own marketing consultancy, moved back to Singapore, organized B2B communities and CXO dinners, and eventually found my place in SaaS marketing.

Along the way, I led more than 30 community events, supported GTM initiatives, built partnerships, and discovered how powerful meaningful communities can be.

Every chapter looked different.

Yet every chapter taught me something I still use today.

The biggest lesson?

Your career doesn't need to be linear to be meaningful.

Curiosity compounds.

The more experiences you collect, the more perspectives you gain.

Today, the work I enjoy most is building brands, bringing thoughtful people together, and helping meaningful communities grow.

name: Medha Thakkar
body:
The business community space is growing faster than most people realize.

A few numbers stand out.

• More than 76% of professionals say their best business opportunities come through in-person networking.

• Community-led businesses are growing significantly faster than traditional service businesses.

• Event-based communities are projected to become a trillion-dollar industry over the next decade.

Behind these statistics is an even more interesting trend.

Many founders now acquire their first customers through communities rather than cold outreach or paid advertising.

We've seen this pattern before.

The creator economy changed how individuals built audiences.

Community-first businesses are beginning to reshape how founders build companies.

Communities are no longer simply audiences.

They're ecosystems where trust, relationships, education, and business happen simultaneously.

My belief is that community-led businesses will become one of the defining models of modern entrepreneurship.

Not because they're trendy.

Because trust has become one of the most valuable business assets anyone can build.

name: Sidhaant K
body:
I often see business owners unaware that they may owe Fringe Benefits Tax (FBT).

Many assume that a work vehicle is automatically exempt, that occasional personal use doesn't matter, or that electric vehicles are always outside the scope of FBT.

The reality is different.

If a work vehicle is garaged at an employee's home, that generally counts as private use and FBT may apply.

Other employee benefits—including laptops, gym memberships, and employer-paid meals—can also attract FBT depending on the circumstances.

And from 1 April 2025, the exemption for Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs) no longer applies in many cases.

The ATO is currently reviewing businesses that may have overlooked or incorrectly reported FBT relating to work vehicles.

With the FBT year ending on 31 March 2026, there is still time to review your position.

I recommend taking a few practical steps:

• Review all benefits provided to employees during the year.
• Check whether any PHEVs in your fleet now attract FBT.
• Ensure your FBT return is accurate before lodgment.

Proactive review is far less expensive than reactive correction.

Strong compliance protects your business, reduces unnecessary regulatory exposure, and provides greater confidence moving forward.

name: Sidhaant K
body:
Selecting an accounting or bookkeeping provider based solely on accuracy is one of the most common mistakes I see.

Accuracy is important.

But accuracy is only the baseline.

Every competent accounting professional—and every modern accounting system—is expected to deliver compliant, accurate financial records.

The real value clients are paying for is certainty.

Certainty is knowing your finances are being managed with expertise, accountability, and foresight.

It's the confidence that allows you to make business decisions without constantly checking, worrying, or second-guessing the numbers.

Technical skill alone doesn't create that confidence.

Communication does.

Ownership does.

Responsiveness does.

A great accounting partner explains complex matters in plain language, responds promptly, presents practical options instead of instructions, and helps you feel informed rather than overwhelmed.

I've seen technically brilliant providers leave business owners frustrated because they lacked clarity and proactive communication.

I've also seen providers create tremendous value simply because clients trusted them completely.

When evaluating accounting support, remember:

You're not paying for accuracy alone.

You're paying for the certainty that accuracy creates.

name: Sidhaant K
body:
Outsourcing should create leverage.

Yet many firms discover the opposite.

Instead of reducing workload, outsourcing creates more follow-ups, more revisions, and more oversight.

In most cases, the issue isn't outsourcing itself.

It's how it's structured.

When work is reduced to isolated tasks and people are treated as interchangeable resources, ownership disappears.

Without ownership, accountability weakens.

Your internal team inevitably steps back in to explain, review, and correct.

What was supposed to improve efficiency becomes another process to manage.

The better approach is to design for ownership.

Give your offshore team responsibility—not just tasks.

Help them understand the broader context, the expected outcome, and how their work contributes to the firm's success.

Treat them as an extension of your practice rather than a separate support function.

When ownership exists, something changes.

The team begins solving problems instead of waiting for instructions.

Follow-ups reduce.

Decisions improve.

Work returns with greater consistency and accountability.

At that point, outsourcing stops being about reducing costs.

It becomes a strategic advantage that allows your firm to scale sustainably.

name: Sidhaant K
body:
One of the questions I hear most often from Australian business owners is:

'Is there anything we can do to reduce tax before the financial year ends?'

The difficulty is that this question usually arrives in May or June.

By then, many of the decisions that determine the final tax outcome have already been made.

Effective tax planning doesn't happen at the end of the financial year.

It happens throughout it.

Hiring staff.

Purchasing equipment.

Timing business expenses.

Drawing funds from the business.

Each decision influences your eventual tax position.

I've worked with businesses generating similar revenue but paying very different amounts of tax.

The difference wasn't hidden deductions.

It was planning.

Successful tax strategies are rarely dramatic.

They're built through consistent, well-timed financial decisions made across the entire year.

When tax planning becomes part of your regular business strategy instead of an annual exercise, you gain more control, make stronger decisions, and avoid unnecessary surprises when year-end arrives.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
Our platform processes 2.5 million queries per second, 180 billion a day. I want to explain what that number actually represents, because "queries per second" sounds abstract until you see what has to happen inside each one.

Every single ad impression opportunity, someone opening an app, loading a page, a connected TV starting a show, triggers a real-time auction. Our system has to evaluate that specific opportunity, decide whether to bid, calculate the right price, and respond, all within roughly 100 milliseconds.

At our volume, that's not one decision happening carefully.

It's millions of simultaneous, independent decisions, each one factoring in targeting criteria, budget pacing, brand safety checks, and bid strategy, without any single decision getting to slow down and think.

The actual engineering problem was never making one good decision well. Any reasonably competent team can do that. The problem is making millions of good decisions per second without the infrastructure itself becoming the bottleneck, because a slow ad server doesn't produce a bad decision. It produces a missed opportunity, silently, repeated billions of times a day, with nobody outside the platform ever noticing it happened.

Most advertisers never think about this layer at all, and they shouldn't have to. It's one of the invisible engineering problems in this industry: doing the same complex judgment call correctly, at a volume most software never has to handle, entirely behind the scenes.

Well... I just described the problem ASTRAD solves.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
We've never raised outside funding. Every server, every hire, every ad exchange integration has come from customer revenue since day one in 2019.

I didn't plan it that way initially  - started as necessity, we simply didn't have the network to raise early, and became conviction once I actually watched what it protected.

The honest version: building this category is expensive (genuinely) before it's profitable. Real-time bidding infrastructure, compliance across dozens of regions, ad exchange integrations that take months to build properly.

Most competitors funded that build with VC money. But we funded it more slowly, with early customers betting on an unfinished platform before it deserved that bet.

Two things that constraint actually gave us:

i. A habit of shipping only what advertisers were genuinely asking for

ii.  A complete lack of pressure to hit a growth number someone else's fund timeline required.

I won't pretend it's been comfortable. Slower growth, tighter margins in the early years, real stretches where a funding round would have made the next quarter considerably easier.

I'd still choose it again. In a category where a lot of competitors are subsidizing growth with investor money, we only ever had to answer to the people actually writing us checks.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
For most of programmatic advertising's history, the good tools have been gatekept behind a minimum spend line. Six figures a year, sometimes more, just to get a login.

It's a business model choice, and it's the specific thing that made me start ASTRAD in 2019.

A 40-person DTC brand and a Fortune 500 advertiser are, technically, trying to solve very similar problem: reach the right person, on the right device, at the right moment, without wasting spend on people who'll never buy.

The tech to do that at scale existed. Access to it didn't, unless you already had a large enough budget to be worth a DSP's sales team's time.

That gatekeeping wasn't really about the smaller advertiser being unprofitable to serve. That was about legacy platforms built around high-touch, high-minimum enterprise sales, where a lean self-serve model simply wasn't the business they were built to run.

We built ASTRAD specifically without that minimum.

Self-serve access, real targeting depth, the same 40+ ad exchange reach a large advertiser gets, available to a company running a five-figure annual budget.

I don't think every advertiser needs a managed enterprise relationship. I also do think every advertiser deserves access to the same underlying technology, regardless of how large the check is.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
When an ABM campaign underperforms, the first question almost everyone asks is: was the targeting precise enough.

Wrong question, most of the time.

The better question: did every account on this list get treated as equally important, when they obviously weren't?

Real ABM requires tiering. A short list of high-value accounts deserves personalized creative, sequential multi-channel touches, real coordination with whoever's doing outreach on the sales side. A longer list of lower-priority accounts deserves a lighter, more automated version of the same idea.

What actually happens most often: the budget and creative production time gets split evenly across the entire account list, because tiering feels harder to justify internally than just running one consistent campaign for everyone on it.

The accounts running this well don't have more sophisticated targeting technology than everyone else. They have a shorter tier-one list and the discipline to treat it differently from everything below it.

Ask which question your last underperforming ABM campaign was actually built to answer. If it wasn't the tiering question - that's probably where the fix is sitting.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
Before: buying a specific billboard for a specific month, hoping the right people happened to drive past it, with no way to know until the campaign was already over whether it actually worked.

After: the same physical screen, now sitting behind a real-time bidding layer, targetable by device signals and movement patterns, measurable the same way a digital display campaign always has been.

The screens haven't changed much. The layer behind them, though, has changed completely.

That shift matters most for ABM specifically. A DOOH screen near a specific office building used to be generic local advertising. Combined with device-level targeting, it now becomes a genuine ABM channel, reaching actual decision-makers based on real-world movement.

Most advertisers still buy DOOH the old way: a flat placement with no real-time optimization and no connection to their other digital channels. The ones actually getting ahead are treating it as just another programmatic channel inside a broader cross-device strategy, not a separate line item bought through a completely different process.

The physical screen is the least interesting part of this change. The interesting part is that DOOH inventory now behaves like every other programmatic channel: measurable, targetable, and optimizable in real time, which changes what it's actually capable of doing inside a serious campaign.

Not a bad time to be in ad tech.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
6,000 to 10,000 ads a day.

That's the estimate for how many ads the average person now sees.

Make no mistake, I'm not talking about clicks or conversions. I'm talking about exposure, filtered out by a brain that had to build a defence mechanism against sensory overload.

Most creative briefs still optimise for polish. Clean brand guidelines, consistent color palette, a message everyone on the internal team agrees reads well.

None of that helps against a filter this practiced.

What actually gets through is "specificity".

A message so precise to one exact situation that a generic filter can't confidently auto-reject it the way it rejects anything that reads like every other ad in the category.

Polish is table stakes now. It was never the thing that got you noticed. Specificity was always doing that work. Most brands just haven't needed to admit it until the exposure number got this absurd.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
We give advertisers over 50 targeting options on our platform. I want to say something slightly against our own product here: most campaigns fail not from too little targeting, but from stacking too many targeting layers at once.

Signs your campaign is over-targeted, from what I've watched across thousands of accounts:

(1) Daily impression delivery is a fraction of your budget's actual capacity

(2) Performance metrics stay flat week over week, no real optimization curve visible

(3) You're layering geo, device, behavioral, and contextual targeting simultaneously, on day one

(4) Your audience size estimate, before the campaign even launches, is under six figures

(5) You added a new targeting layer specifically because a previous one alone "felt too broad"

(6) Nobody on the team can explain, in one sentence, which single targeting dimension is actually doing the most work

If three or more of these are true, the fix usually is fewer targeting layers, enough good volume for the system to learn, and adding precision back in only once there's actual performance data to justify it.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
We offer three ways to work with Astrad: self-serve, managed, and white-label. I get asked constantly which one a given company should choose, and my answer has almost nothing to do with budget size.

(1) Self-serve fits a team with solid in-house programmatic expertise, someone who wants direct control over bidding and targeting decisions and doesn't need strategic guidance layered on top.

(2) Managed fits a team with marketing goals but no dedicated programmatic specialist in-house. They need someone translating strategy into actual campaign execution and not just a login.

(3) White-label fits a different buyer entirely: agencies and platforms wanting to offer programmatic advertising under their own brand, without building the underlying DSP infrastructure themselves.

The mistake I see most often is a company choosing based on budget alone, assuming self-serve is for smaller spenders and managed is for larger ones. That's backwards. A well-funded company with zero in-house programmatic expertise needs managed service regardless of budget size, and a lean team with real expertise can run self-serve effectively on a modest budget.

Make sure to match the model to the actual expertise in the room - not the size of the number in the budget line.

name: Daniel Macià
body:
Most platforms in programmatic advertising treat brand safety as a compliance requirement -  a checkbox to satisfy regulators and reassure legal teams.

That "framing" undersells what brand safety actually protects.

A brand safety failure isn't just a regulatory risk. There are about an ad appearing next to content that actively damages the exact trust a brand spent years and real budget building.

That's a considerably far more expensive mistake than a compliance failure, and it's rarely the part of the conversation anyone leads with.

We built our own safety tooling in-house, layered on top of external partnerships, specifically because relying purely on third-party verification means your safety standard is only as sharp as your least specific partner's, applied identically to every client regardless of that specific client's actual risk tolerance.

Different brands have different safety thresholds. A financial services client's tolerance for adjacent controversial content looks nothing like a consumer lifestyle brand's. And treating the same rules for every brand ignores those differences and leaves some brands exposed to risks they never wanted to take.

I'd rather compete on protecting a client's specific brand risk profile than compete purely on reach and pricing. Reach without safety discipline is just a bigger surface area for something to go wrong - and in our category, it happens again and again and again.

name: Brian Hamor
body:
I don't have a co-founder right now. Some days that might be a genuine advantage but most days it's just harder than the polished version of this story usually lets on.

The advantage is: every product decision, every pricing call, every pivot happens at the speed of one person's conviction. Early-stage speed is underrated, and solo founding is, in a narrow sense, faster.

The cost is also real, and I don't think enough solo founders say this part out loud. There's no one in the building who carries the same weight of the outcome that I do. A hire cares. An advisor cares. Neither of them wakes up at 3am doing payroll math the way a co-founder would, because it isn't actually their company the same way it's mine.

I've started actively building a small group of other solo, bootstrapped founders specifically to fill part of that gap, not a co-founder replacement, but people who understand the specific weight of a decision resting on one person's judgment with no one else in the room who has to live with it the same way.

If you're solo-founding something right now and haven't built that group yet, it's worth the effort. I wish I'd built mine sooner.

name: Brian Hamor
body:
Waiting for the day someone posts a weekly LinkedIn update from inside an actual job and it just says: "Week 14. Still here. Nothing broke. Bonus math unchanged."

Every founder update is milestones, wins, momentum. Every actual week at a real job is mostly just... showing up and doing the work competently, which is somehow the least postable version of professional life that exists.

I say this as someone who posts founder content constantly. I'm aware of the irony.

The useful founder posts, the ones I actually learn something from reading, are rarely the milestone announcements. They're the ones admitting a specific week that was just okay. A deal that stalled for a boring reason. A feature that shipped a week late because the actual scoping took longer than expected, not because of some dramatic pivot.

I don't think the answer is faking more mundane content for authenticity points. That's its own kind of performance. I do think the platform would be a little more useful, and a little less exhausting, if "solid, unremarkable week, still building" was a genuinely acceptable post instead of something everyone's quietly living through and nobody's writing.

name: Brian Hamor
body:
Win-loss analysis as a consulting category has existed for years. Most of it, in my honest opinion, is built backwards.

The traditional model: hire a consultant, they interview a sample of closed deals once, quarterly or annually, and deliver a report. By the time that report lands, the specific deals it's analyzing are ancient history, and the insights arrive too late to actually save any of the revenue they're describing.

(1) Sampling instead of covering every deal means you're only ever seeing a curated slice, usually whichever deals were easiest to get someone to talk about.

(2) Quarterly cadence means the insight arrives long after the sales team has already moved on, emotionally and practically, from the deals being discussed.

(3) A static report gets read once, maybe discussed in one meeting, and then filed away, rather than actually changing behavior on the next hundred deals moving through the pipeline right now.

What convinced me this needed rebuilding was watching consultants I respected produce smart reports that changed nothing, because the insight and the moment it could actually be acted on had already drifted too far apart by the time anyone read it.

Win-loss feedback has to be continuous and immediate to actually change anything. Quarterly and retrospective was never going to do that, no matter how sharp the analysis inside the report actually was.

name: Brian Hamor
body:
We just launched something I haven't talked about publicly yet: a white-label win-loss program.

Agencies and consultants can now run win-loss analysis for their own clients under their own brand, with BuyerExperience running the backend.

Here's why we built it, and why now specifically.

(1) I kept getting inbound from sales consultants and fractional RevOps people who wanted to offer win-loss analysis as a service line, but had no interest in building the actual infrastructure to collect and analyze it at scale.

(2) Building that infrastructure properly, outreach sequencing, transcript analysis, scoring models, is a multi-year investment. Most consultancies correctly don't want to become a software company just to offer one service line.

(3) We already built it. Letting a partner put their own name on the output, while we run everything behind the scenes, is a faster path to the same outcome for everyone involved than either side building it alone.

This is a different bet than our direct product. It succeeds or fails based on whether partners can actually sell it convincingly to their own client base, not on our own sales motion at all.

Early days. I'll actually know if this was the right call in about two quarters, once real partner-sourced revenue either shows up or doesn't.

name: Brian Hamor
body:
People assume "automated closed-lost feedback" means we send a survey link and hope someone fills it out. That's not it, and the difference matters.

Here's what actually happens when a deal gets marked lost in a customer's CRM:

(1) A trigger fires, tied to the specific deal - not a generic monthly batch job.

(2) Outreach goes out from a neutral third party, not the losing vendor. Buyers tell a stranger the truth about why they said no far more often than they tell the actual rep who just lost the deal.

(3) The conversation, when a buyer engages, gets structured around specific categories: discovery quality, product fit, demo execution, pricing conversation timing. Not "how did we do," which gets you a polite non-answer almost every time.

(4) That structured feedback gets scored and fed back into the CRM against the actual account, not left sitting in a separate report nobody opens.

The uncomfortable truth about win-loss feedback is that a buyer will almost never tell the person who just lost their business the real reason. They'll tell someone else. The entire mechanism has to be built around that fact, not around convenience for the vendor asking.

Most win-loss programs fail because they skip step two entirely and wonder why response quality is so thin.

name: Brian Hamor
body:
Every sales leader I talk to assumes reps don't revisit closed-lost accounts because they're lazy or disorganized. I don't think that's the actual reason, and treating it as the reason produces the wrong fix.

The actual reason, in my experience talking to a lot of reps directly: revisiting a lost deal feels like admitting it was lost in the first place, in front of a manager who might ask why it took this long to circle back. There's a real, quiet social cost to raising your hand on an old loss, even when the upside of reactivating it is genuinely good for everyone.

That's a culture problem wearing a process costume. You can build the best automated reminder system in the world, and it still won't get used if reps feel like acting on it exposes something they'd rather leave buried in a CRM nobody's actively reviewing.

What's worked - watching customers use our platform successfully versus not: leadership explicitly reframing a reactivated deal as a genuine win worth celebrating, not a quiet correction to an old mistake. Teams that make that reframe out loud, in their own sales meetings, see meaningfully higher reactivation rates than teams that just turn a tool on and expect behavior to change on its own.

Don't confuse solving the memory problem with solving the psychology problem. Technology can do the first, but never the second on its own.

name: Brian Hamor
body:
A prospective customer asked me directly last month: why should I trust a small company with our most sensitive sales data, every reason our biggest deals fell apart.

Fair question. I've thought about how to answer it honestly, not just reassuringly.

The honest answer isn't "we're too small to be a target" or "trust us, we're careful." But being small right now means every single customer relationship is disproportionately important to us in a way it simply isn't at a larger, more established vendor. A data incident at a company our size doesn't get absorbed quietly into a large customer base. It's existential.

That's the actual, specific incentive structure a prospective customer should be evaluating, not our marketing copy about security. A company where losing your trust could end the business behaves very differently than one where it's a bad quarter.

I'd rather make that argument directly than pretend our size is an advantage on trust. What it does mean is that our incentive to protect that data is about as high as it's possible for a vendor's incentive to be, because we honestly don't have the cushion a bigger company does if we get it wrong.

name: Paul Roiter
body:
Before Xelix, Nick and I built a peer-to-peer ticketing app called Dingo. 

The idea was simple: let people resell tickets at or below face value instead of through a scalper. We got press coverage, a spot in the Evening Standard, a mention in TechCrunch, and for about 6 months it felt like we'd found something worthy.

The unit economics never worked. Every ticket we processed cost us more to move through the platform than the platform actually made back, and no amount of press coverage fixes a business where the core transaction loses money. 

We shut it down in 2015, quietly, without a press release this time.

What that failure taught me had nothing to do with tickets. It was that a good story and a working business are two completely separate things, and it's dangerously easy to confuse the first for evidence of the second when journalists are calling and the app is climbing download charts. 

I spent the next few years doing investment analysis at Velos Partners specifically because I wanted to get better at telling the difference before I built anything else, looking at other people's businesses and asking the boring, unglamorous question: does the actual transaction make money, not does the story sound good.

When Phil and I started Xelix in 2018, the first thing we did was sitting with a spreadsheet and forcing ourselves to answer, in plain numbers, what a customer would actually pay for and whether we could deliver it for less than that. 

It's a less exciting way to start a company than a TechCrunch mention. It's also the reason Xelix is still here and Dingo isn't.

name: Paul Roiter
body:
I've now had the same conversation with 100s of finance leaders over seven years, and there's a pattern in how Accounts Payable gets treated that I don't think gets said plainly enough: AP is almost never a priority until the exact moment it becomes an emergency.

A duplicate payment goes out. A vendor statement reveals thousands of dollars of missed credit notes. A fraud attempt nearly clears because nobody caught the change in bank details. 

Only then does a CFO ask why nobody was watching this closely enough, and the honest answer is usually that AP was never resourced to watch closely in the first place. It's treated as a processing function - right up until the moment a control failure costs money.

The number that still surprises finance leaders when I share it: our Financial Leakage Report puts the AP opportunity at around $53 billion, duplicates, invoice errors, missed credit notes, and fraud quietly draining value from finance teams who genuinely believe their existing controls have this covered. 

Most of them don't find out how much is actually leaking until they run a proper audit against their transaction data, instead of assuming their ERP's built-in duplicate check is already doing the job.

What has changed the conversation more than any pitch we've ever built is showing finance leaders their own leakage number before they sign anything. 

Nobody argues with their own data the way they'll argue with a vendor's general claim about industry averages. 

The moment AP stops being an abstract cost center and starts being a specific, provable number sitting on their own books, the conversation about priorities changes on its own.

name: Paul Roiter
body:
I get asked constantly, usually by someone slightly nervous about the answer, whether AI is going to replace Accounts Payable teams. 

My honest answer disappoints people looking for a dramatic prediction either way. 

But here's my take:

The manual, repetitive parts of AP, matching invoices to POs, chasing a vendor for a missing statement, flagging a duplicate that a human reviewer would catch eventually anyway, are genuinely well suited to automation, and we've built a business on specific that premise. 

What's harder to automate, and what I don't think gets enough credit in the doom-and-boom takes about AI replacing finance, is judgment: deciding whether an unusual payment pattern is actually fraud or just an unusual but legitimate business reason, deciding how hard to push a vendor relationship over a disputed statement, deciding which control gap is actually worth fixing this quarter versus next year.

What I've watched happen at our best customers is the same people spending their time on that judgment work instead of the repetitive matching that used to consume most of their week. The AP manager who used to spend three days a month manually reconciling statements now spends that time investigating the patterns the reconciliation surfaces, which is a meaningfully different, more valuable job than the one they had before - not a smaller version of it.

I'd rather be honest that this transition is genuinely uneven across companies right now than pretend every finance team is there. Some are still fighting to get basic automation approved internally. But the direction is clear enough, after seven years watching this up close, that I'm comfortable saying the fear of AI replacing the AP function is aimed at the wrong target. The function isn't disappearing. The repetitive half of it is, and what's left is considerably more interesting work for the people doing it.

name: Alisa McPhail
body:
I joined Xelix in 2019 as its first dedicated marketing hire, when the company was 8 people. I grew that function, built the brand, put a proper tech stack in place, and helped take the company from Seed through Series A. 

In 2022, I left for a global marketing role.

A few months later I was back at Xelix, this time as Head of Marketing - joining a company that had grown considerably in my absence and needed the function rebuilt again for a completely different stage of the business. 

Going from 8 people to 40 is a different marketing problem than scaling a marketing team that already exists but needs a sharper strategy and a bigger remit. I'd solved the first problem once already. The second one required different instincts/direction.
